en: The Sublime Commentary on the Sutra of Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life,
Scroll One,
composed by the Śramaṇa Zhili of Siming during the Song Dynasty.
Regarding this commentary on the meaning of the sutra, because people desire pure retribution, those who preach and listen to it have been numerous.

The Master Baoyun, from whom [this tradition] was received, first composed the record; following his lead down to the present day, the production of commentaries has never ceased. All of them take Zhiyi as their authority—how could there be anyone among them who does not know the wondrous contemplation for cultivating the mind and the textual meaning of the response to the four pure lands?

It is truly because his compassion for sentient beings was profound and his skillful wisdom was well-suited to the times that he spoke extensively on the characteristics of phenomena while showing few meditation gates; his primary concern was that even ordinary people at the lowest level might universally receive the seeds of their karmic conditions.

In this auspicious era, the Perfect Vehicle (Paryaya-yāna) is being extensively expounded; those who aspire to its study all desire to grasp its essential meaning for the sake of cultivation and realization.
Therefore, I have exhausted my humble thoughts to compile several thousand words, following the "Exquisite Commentary" (*Miaozong*) above to provide a brief elucidation of this sub-commentary.

The skill of seizing the opportune moment is not within my power; my wish is simply that all who possess a heart may practice mindfulness of the Buddha. This is the reason for the composition of this commentary.
Written on the Double Ninth day of the fifth year of the Tianxi era, the year of Xinyou. Thus ends the preface.

Regarding this title of the commentary, the eight characters beginning with "Buddha" (佛) fully enumerate the titles of the sūtras, all of which are the objects of explanation; only the single character "commentary" (疏) is that which explains them.
The present five chapters explain these eight characters; their meaning is somewhat detailed and will be evident upon entering the text itself.
If you wish to know in advance, you may state the general outline.
"Sūtra" is the universal designation, while the others are specific names.
For now, I shall clarify the specific ones.
“Spoken by the Buddha” refers to the transformation master Śākyamuni proclaiming and expounding [the teaching] through his four types of eloquence.
“Contemplation” (guan) is a general designation for the subject that contemplates, namely, the sixteen contemplations.
"Amitāyus Buddha" refers to the essential object of contemplation that subsumes the fifteen realms.
Setting aside the subject who speaks for a moment, let us briefly clarify what is spoken.
The contemplating subject is always the single mind with its three modes of contemplation (*sankuan*), and the contemplated object is always the single realm of the three truths (*sandì*).
Vairocana pervades all places; all phenomena are the Buddha-dharma.

What are called sentient beings are Buddhas by virtue of their inherent nature; they are neither self nor other, neither cause nor effect, but are the very essence of perfect and eternal great awakening.
Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "That which is called the meaning of 'awakening' refers to the essence of the mind being free from thought.
This state of being free from thought is equal to the realm of empty space, pervading everywhere without exception."
"The single characteristic of the Dharma-realm is precisely the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding Dharma-body; based on this Dharma-body, it is termed 'original enlightenment' (benjue).
Thus we know that the perfectly luminous essence of the Buddha of fruition is the inherent nature-virtue (xingde) possessed by us ordinary beings from the very beginning.

Therefore, among all the practices taught in the various teachings, there is none that does not aim to reveal this very essence of awakening; thus, the four samādhis are collectively termed "Buddhānusmṛti" (Mindfulness of the Buddha), though their specific contemplative methods differ as entryways.
In the *Ekavyūha-samādhi*, one directly contemplates the three paths to manifest the Buddha of the original nature;
in the *Vaipulya-samādhi*, one contemplates the *dhāraṇī* to manifest it;

in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one combines reciting the sutra; in the *Avalokiteśvara-samādhi*, one combines counting the breaths; and in the *Bodhyaṅga-samādhi*, one traverses the three natures through mindfulness.
Regarding these samādhis, although the activities they involve differ, the mindfulness of the Buddha is the same, for all serve to manifest the essence of Great Enlightenment.
Although all involve mindfulness of the Buddha, this is the general path for manifesting the essence of all Buddhas.

If this gate of contemplation and the Pratyutpanna Samādhi rely upon the environment and inhabitants of that Land of Peaceful Nurturing, employing subtle and wondrous observation, they focus exclusively on Amitābha to reveal the true body of the Buddha.
Although one may take refuge in those objective realms, one must know that the environment and its inhabitants coexist within a single mind.
The nature of the mind is all-pervasive; there is no phenomenon it does not create and no phenomenon it does not possess.
If even a single hair’s breadth of a phenomenon were to arise outside of the mind, it could not be called Mahayana contemplation.
The practitioner should know that by relying on the nature of the mind to contemplate the environment and its inhabitants, the environment and inhabitants can be clearly manifested;
by relying on the environment and inhabitants to contemplate the nature of the mind, the nature of the mind is easily brought forth.

Regarding the statement that the nature of mind possesses all phenomena and creates all phenomena: in reality, there is no possessor or possessed, nor any creator or created. Mind itself is phenomena, and phenomena themselves are mind; both the causal conditions that create and the phenomena that are created are, in their very place, entirely the nature of mind.

Therefore, when one now contemplates the environment and its inhabitants, it is the mind of the dharma-realm contemplating the objects of the dharma-realm, giving rise to the form and mind of the environment and its inhabitants within the dharma-realm.
This is what is meant by "only the environment and only the inhabitants," "only form and only mind," and "only contemplation and only objects."
Therefore, in explaining the character "contemplation" (guān), one employs the three contemplations within a single mind;
in explaining "Immeasurable Life" (Wúliàngshòu), one employs the three bodies as a single essence.
Since the meanings of essence, doctrine, power, and function all follow the Perfect [Teaching], the classification of the teaching belongs to the Sudden.

The Fivefold Profound Meaning (*Wǔchóng xuányì*) is fundamentally the contemplative method elucidated within the sutra; the Great Master (Zhiyi) pre-emptively extracts it to explain the title of the scripture, desiring that practitioners employ this method of viewing phenomena to enter the sixteen gates for cultivation and realization. Therefore, in the introductory text, he uses the primary to encompass the manifold and the principal to subsume the dependent.
Since the contemplation of the Buddha is itself the three bodies (trikāya), how could the contemplation of other things not be the three truths (trisatya)?
I address practitioners: although this contemplation is profound and subtle, it is fundamentally intended for those at the beginning stage.
If you can advance in your practice, why worry that you will not achieve success?
Even if one has not yet entered the ranks of the sages, the causal power [of such practice] is nonetheless strong.

Upon being born in that land, one will be permitted to participate in the great assembly; what is seen there—both the environment and its inhabitants—is subtle, sublime, and inconceivable. One will swiftly ascend the stages of the noble ones and extensively deliver sentient beings, forever distinguishing this from worldly goodness and the practices of the Hīnayāna.

Those who attain rebirth are like those in this land who have long cultivated their practice to perfection; they perceive signs that are extraordinary amidst the various assemblies and awaken easily to the Dharma upon hearing it.
By analogy with these cases, the merit lies in the *Miaozong* (The Sublime Commentary).
However, because one's merit from observing the precepts is not refined and lacks the vow for rebirth [in a Pure Land], one must remain in this defiled land to hear the Dharma and enter the truth.

One must fear that in the Sahā world, a Buddha is not encountered constantly; even if one meets virtuous friends, if one’s physical and mental faculties are not superior, it is difficult to arouse the bodhicitta. Moreover, as the sensory objects are coarse and powerful, this land is truly a perilous place.

Therefore, one must externally perform ritual repentance and internally apply diligent contemplation of principle; with the primary and auxiliary practices proceeding together, and with vows added as a necessary restraint, one will surely realize non-arising swiftly in the Jewel Land.
The present explanation of the gate of contemplation has its meaning in this.
"Sū" (Commentary) means "to loosen" and "to resolve.
It loosens and opens up the meanings and principles above so that they flow without obstruction, enabling the practitioner to grasp the essential meaning and cultivate it accordingly.
Next is the title of the author, which is fully detailed in the separate biography and various commentaries; those who do not know it must consult those texts.
Second, the explanation of the text.
First, the explanation of the preface, in three parts:
First, the introduction to the intent of the sutra’s contemplation, in two parts:
first, the explicit explanation of the contemplative practice, in two parts:
first, the statement of the intent. Second: [The following section].
First, establishing purity in contrast to defilement, in two parts:
first, the Dharma, in two parts:
first, clarifying the suffering and pleasure of the two types of retribution.
Wishing to discuss contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), one first demonstrates the characteristics of the two types of retribution: suffering and pleasure.
The text contains four phrases, each of which discusses the relative opposition between the pure and the defiled.
The first phrase contrasts the suffering and pleasure of the lands that have been established.
The Pure Land of Peaceful Nurturing receives only various joys, and is therefore called the "Land of Bliss";
the defiled land of Endurance undergoes much suffering, and thus its meaning is described as a "Realm of Suffering.
The second phrase contrasts the nobility and meanness of the entities that constitute these realms.
That [world] consists purely of the seven treasures, which are briefly described as gold and jewels;
this [world] abounds in various impurities, which are briefly spoken of as silt and sand.
The second line contrasts the purity and defilement of the physical substance received at birth.

In this land, the six realms of existence possess all four modes of birth (*yoni*). Among humans now, most are born from the womb. When the mother consumes cold or hot food, or experiences hunger and satiety, the child within the womb suffers as if dwelling in the hells of cold and heat, being inverted, suspended, or crushed by mountains;

hence it is called the "womb-hell. In that land, of the nine grades of rebirth, eight are born from lotuses. Even for those of the lowest grade who must pass through many kalpas—as stated in the *Mūla-sūtra*—they cultivate goodness with a mind free of doubt and are born into that womb-palace where their happiness equals that of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. How much more so for those of the eighth and ninth grades who do not harbor doubts; how could they experience suffering? Therefore, receiving birth in the lotus pond is itself bliss.
The second phrase contrasts the coarse and the fine regarding the places where one dwells after birth;
this refers to thorny thickets and forests on the one hand, and golden channels and jade trees on the other.
Although each of these four phrases contrasts suffering and pleasure, their underlying intent is to contrast impurity with the manifestation of those pure characteristics.
Furthermore, it should be understood that while the text of these four propositions appears to reveal only the two lands of Shared Dwelling (*sahā-vāsa*),

when one examines this in light of the subsequent section— which clarifies the central thesis by fully discussing the characteristics of purity and defilement across all four lands— it is clear that they do not exclusively refer to the land of Shared Dwelling.
One should know that each of the four propositions applies to all four types of purity and defilement:
the lightness or heaviness of afflictions through views and thoughts results in either a blissful realm or a realm of suffering within the Land of Common Residence;
the skillfulness or clumsiness of the methods of "substantiality" and "analysis" results in either a blissful realm or a realm of suffering within the Land of Expedient Means.
Entering either gradually or suddenly, one accordingly experiences the realm of true recompense as a land of bliss or a realm of suffering;
realizing partial or ultimate enlightenment, one accordingly experiences the realm of tranquil light as a land of bliss or a realm of suffering.
By this analogy, it is likewise with gold and jewels versus sand and mud, the womb-prison versus the lotus pond, and the thorny forest versus the jade tree.
Within a single treatise, the main text and the preface must necessarily not contradict one another;
however, because the preface provides a general indication while the main text offers a specific exposition, they appear to differ.
Question:
Since the three lower pure lands all possess characteristics, one may discuss matters such as gold and jewels;
however, the pure land of tranquil light is entirely devoid of characteristics—how then can one speak of golden jewels, lotus ponds, and jade trees?
Answer:

When the sutras and treatises speak of the "tranquil light" (jìguāng) as being without marks (wúxiàng), they mean that it has already exhausted all marks of defilement and obstruction; it is not like empty space where nothing exists at all.
This is because when the three delusions are ultimately purified, the physical environment and its inhabitants, as well as form and mind, become ultimately manifest and luminous.
Therefore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "By the cessation of this form, one attains eternal form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.

The *Renyō-kyō* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) calls these the five aggregates of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā-skandha*). This is also what the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* refers to as the permanence of worldly phenomena. In the *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, it is taught that form and fragrance are none other than the Middle Way. These are, therefore, called the ultimate Land of Bliss, the ultimate gold and jewels, the ultimate lotus pond, and the ultimate jade trees.

Furthermore, because this teaching exhausts the abandonment of defilement and traces the source of the attainment of purity, realms such as the Suffering Domain (Duḥkhaviṣaya) are judged to belong to the three obstacles, while the Land of Bliss, with its golden jewels, is established as the Land of Quiescent Light (Śāntaprabhā).
If one speaks in terms of the equality of purity and defilement, then the ultimate mire and silt of the realm of suffering are themselves the Land of Peaceful Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*).
These two explanations merely accord with the *siddhānta* (the established tenets); there is nothing in them that is not perfectly consummate.
Question:
The Buddha’s unsurpassed retribution is the principle within the phenomenon; thus, one may speak of gold and the like.
Ultimate quiescent radiance is the principle within the phenomenon; how could there be gold and the like therein?
If these were co-existent, then phenomena and principle would be conflated; how, then, could one distinguish between the two lands?
Answer:

The Buddha’s unsurpassed recompense is ultimate initial enlightenment (*ādikṣayajñāna*), and the superior grade of quiescent light is ultimate original enlightenment (*mūlapratyavekṣājñāna*). Since both the initial and the original have reached their ultimate limit, how could they be divided into two distinct entities?

One should understand that although the two lands are distinguished in terms of phenomena and principle, they are in reality neither existent nor non-existent; how could it be that the truly good and wondrous existence is not the principle?
How could the principle of the secret treasury be the same as the "emptiness" of the Lesser Vehicle?

Therefore, these two names—phenomenon and principle—refer to a single essence: because it is the restoration to the original source, it is called the "unsurpassed fruition-phenomenon" (mujō-hōji); because it is the restoration to the original source, it is called the "supreme tranquil light-principle" (jō-saikō-ri).
Therefore, the *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) states:

"The four virtues attained through cultivation and the four virtues inherent from the beginning—when these two meanings are equal, they constitute the characteristics of the body and land of Vairocana.

Furthermore, since the *Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra* (*Jingming shu*) explicitly takes the Land of Tranquil Light (*jiguang*) as the Buddha’s environmental retribution (*yibao*), we know that to insist that the retribution land (*baotu*) definitely possesses gold, jewels, and so forth, while the Land of Tranquil Light definitely lacks them, is to be deluded by the names and entirely ignorant of their meaning.
2. From "Truly because" (*chéng yóu*) onwards, the two types of causal mental conduct are clarified.
"Sincerity" (*chéng*) means reality;
"because of" (*yóu*) means following from.
The purity or defilement of retribution is truly brought about by two causes: the mind and conduct.
"Mind" refers to the two minds of delusion and enlightenment; "conduct" refers to the two types of conduct, contravening or conforming [to the Way].
Within the six realms and the three teachings, one deludes the nature of the Three Virtues and becomes defiled by the three afflictions; therefore, it is called the "defiled mind."
Any physical or verbal actions that contravene principle and are performed with volition are all termed "evil conduct.
Such mental activity brings about rebirth in the four defiled lands, which are characterized by being sunken, coarse, and shallow.
Only through the Perfect and Sudden Teaching—by realizing the nature of the three virtues and detaching from the defilements of the three delusions—is one said to possess a pure mind.
The various actions of body and speech that accord with principle and are performed without artificial effort are called "wholesome conduct.
This mental activity brings about rebirth in the four pure lands, which are loftily elevated and profoundly wondrous.
Although the mind is fundamentally one, because of delusion and awakening, it must be distinguished as defiled or pure.
Although their practices are the same, because they involve either contrariness or compliance, one must distinguish between good and evil.
From these two causes, one receives retribution that is either pure or defiled.

It should be understood that for the person of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), the ultimate realm of quiescent light (*shang jiguang*) serves as the substance of contemplation; thus, all stages of cause—whether ordinary or sage—are identical to the ultimate fruit. This differs from the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), where the practitioner’s aspiration is limited to the twelve grades of the *srotāpanna*, and thus the realization of defilement through partial attainment belongs specifically to the Separate Teaching.
Question:
The ultimate principle is subtle and wondrous, neither defiled nor pure, and involves neither grasping nor rejecting.

Now, by establishing defilement and purity to cause people to grasp and reject, you deviate from this subtle principle; thus, it cannot be the Supreme Vehicle. How, then, can this be called "the wondrous contemplation for cultivating the mind that reveals the one true reality"?
Answer:
To seek the meaning based on the name, one will not find it once in ten thousand cases;
to determine the name based on the meaning, one will not err once in ten thousand cases.

Since the terminology established for what lies outside and within principle, for the Small and Great Vehicles, and for the gradual and sudden-perfect teachings is for the most part similar, one must first determine what is internal and external by distinguishing between the heterodox and the orthodox; next, distinguish the small and the great by means of emptiness and the Middle Way; and finally, distinguish the distinct and the perfect by means of the gradual and the sudden. Only then can these terms be used without the slightest confusion, so that one may rely upon them to establish contemplative practice.

Therefore, our school now evaluates these meanings and employs six propositions to determine their similarities and differences; namely, "mutual sublation," "mutual cultivation," and "mutual identity," each having two propositions, which constitute the six propositions.
Now, using these six criteria, we shall judge this contradiction. First, we shall define its identical names according to their distinct meanings:

namely, the non-defiled and non-pure view of annihilationism held by the non-Buddhists; the realization of the non-defiled and non-pure principle of emptiness by the Two Vehicles; the gate of the non-defiled and non-pure "Middle Only" (*butong zhong*) of the Distinct Teaching; and the principle of the non-defiled and non-pure secret treasury of the Perfect Teaching.

Furthermore, there are four kinds of purity: the view of outsiders who delight in aversion and cling to the notion of purity; the realization of the Two Vehicles through the extinction of delusions; the gateway of gradual purification by departing from defilement in the Separate Teaching; and the principle of immediate purification within defilement in the Perfect Teaching.
Having understood this, one may then discuss the phrases concerning purity and the mutual sublation of the non-defiled and non-pure.
In the sudden purification of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), the non-defiled and non-pure of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), the Two Vehicles, and the external paths are sublated.
The Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) is neither defiled nor pure, thereby subverting the three kinds of purity.
Regarding the phrase "cultivating through characteristics": the three kinds of purity cultivate the secret treasury of the Perfect Teaching, which is neither defiled nor pure;
the three kinds of being neither defiled nor pure cultivate the purity that is identical to defilement within the Perfect Teaching.
Regarding the phrase "the identity of characteristics": in the Perfect Teaching, the purity within defilement is precisely the secret treasury that is neither defiled nor pure;
the secret treasury that is neither defiled nor pure is precisely the purity within defilement.
The wondrous contemplation of the present [sūtra] consists precisely in contemplating the four pure lands within the defiled mind.
Since it illuminates the *jigguang* (light of stillness), how could it differ from the secret treasury (*guizang*) that is neither defiled nor pure?

If you claim that this sūtra’s practice of abandoning the foul and taking up the pure contradicts the principle of the secret treasury’s “double negation” (*shuangfei*), then for what reason did Vaidehī, upon hearing the contemplation of the pure land, realize a partial awakening to the secret treasury?

It should be understood that the present purification of the pure by means of the impure is the establishment of a Pure Land through the principle of the equality of the impure and the pure; this is what is meant by the phrase "the partial meaning being perfected."

However, because the karmic conditions are such that the defiled mind is strong, it is appropriate to purify all phenomena through the gate of purity; therefore, what is now discussed regarding purity does not at all contradict being neither defiled nor pure.
Furthermore, it should be understood that taking and rejecting, when carried to their ultimate limit, are not different from non-taking and non-rejecting.
Of the two metaphors, the straightness of form represents the pure cause—the realization of the intrinsically pure mind and the performance of wholesome deeds in accordance with principle;
the straightness of the shadow represents the fruit, which is the four pure lands.
The turbidity of the source is a metaphor for the defiled cause: the deluded nature, the stained mind, and unwholesome conduct that contravenes principle.
The murkiness of the flow is a metaphor for the result: the four types of impure lands.
If one reverses these metaphors—just as a crooked form produces a concave reflection—they can naturally illustrate the causes and results of contrary cultivation.
If one reverses the preceding metaphors, such that the source is pure and the flow is clear, these may likewise serve as metaphors for practicing the causes and effects in accordance with the Dharma.
Now, two metaphors are presented, each illustrating one aspect; their meaning is thus very clear.
2. From "Therefore, we know" onwards, the practice is shown in relation to the pure.
Having already manifested the characteristics of purity by contrasting them with the impure above, the method of cultivation is now clarified by means of the pure.
The two causes previously indicated were described generally as a pure mind and virtuous conduct.
This passage clarifies the characteristics of cultivation; therefore, it specifically points to the sixteen sublime contemplations and the three types of pure karma currently under discussion.
If one does not illuminate the three truths within the sixteen objects of perception, how can one be said to clarify wondrous contemplation?
To cultivate the three kinds of merit while being defiled by the three delusions does not accord with pure karma.

Wondrous contemplation is the primary practice, while pure karma serves as its aid; when the primary and the auxiliary are practiced in conjunction, they can evoke the four kinds of Land of Ultimate Bliss and enable one to behold the World-Honored Amitābha in his three bodies.

The text explains through mutual correspondence: contemplating the treatise gives rise to the land, and discussing karma leads to seeing the Buddha; since both the primary and secondary [aspects] are present together, the principal and auxiliary are not separated.
Second, from "However, the transformation... onwards, the text is presented in two parts:
first, showing the emergence of the teaching. [End of section]
First, the origins of its flourishing:
The transformation that transcends the mundane must rely on proximate matters to achieve a grand progression;
the teaching that elucidates principle must depend upon opportune conditions to arise.
The status of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) serves as a gradual stage, applicable to all forms of transformation.
The present transformation is specific to the matter of parricide and regicide, intended to cause sentient beings to weary of this defiled world.

This teaching is suited to the capacity of the recipient; it is for Vaidehī—whose name means "Contemplation" in the language of China—because she was skilled in the cultivation of meditative visualization.
2. From "The Great Sage" (*mahāmuni*) onwards, the manifestation of the land is clarified.
The Buddha is the ultimate sage; therefore, he is called "Great.
His compassion extends downward to all beings; thus, it is termed "hanging down" (*chui*).
Entrusting himself to the request of Vaidehī, he expounded the principles he had realized; this is called "expounding the Dharma according to the capacities of beings.

Regarding the phrase "shining with the jade-like marks" and so forth, the Sūtra says: "At that time, the World-Honored One emitted a light from between his eyebrows, which shone throughout immeasurable worlds in the ten directions, then returned and rested upon the crown of the Buddha’s head, transforming into a golden platform as large as Mount Sumeru."

Regarding the phrase "Although he extensively displays," the Sūtra says: "The wondrous lands of the ten directions all appear therein; some lands are composed of the seven treasures, while others consist entirely of lotus flowers."
...and so on, until it says: "At that time, Vaidehī said to the Buddha:
'Although these lands are pure, I now wish to be born in the world of Ultimate Bliss, in the presence of Amitābha Buddha.'"
2. Regarding the section beginning with "Causing the vulgar... and below, it demonstrates the characteristics of contemplation, which is divided into two parts.
First, the general heading: "Causing the vulgar...
and so forth refers to the Sūtra’s statement: "The Tathāgata now instructs Vaidehī and all sentient beings of future ages to contemplate the Western World of Ultimate Bliss."
"By the power of the Buddha, you shall behold that pure land," and so forth.

Second, from the section on "the setting sun" onwards, the sixteen contemplative methods (*ṣoḍaśa-vipaśyanā*) are specifically presented; they do not exceed three categories: namely, the environment (*pratiṣṭhāna*), the inhabitants (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and the rebirth of the three grades of practitioners.
Now, following these three [categories], I shall present them by summarizing the essentials.
The text itself is divided into three parts:
first, the environment (niśraya-vipāka).
First, one contemplates the setting sun as being like a suspended drum, causing the mind to remain steadfastly fixed so that the visualization does not shift.
This has two purposes:

first, to prevent the mind contemplating the sun from wandering; second, to cause the mental image to proceed directly toward the West. Therefore, it is said: "This serves to mark out the direction for sending forth the visualization."
Next, one contemplates clear water and further imagines it becoming ice.
This is because that land has lapis lazuli for its ground; since this ground is difficult to visualize, one first causes one to imagine ice.
Once the visualization of ice is perfected, the precious ground can be seen; therefore, it is said, "In reality, it manifests as a ground of lapis lazuli."

Next, regarding the visualization of the trees, the sutra merely states: "All those jewel trees are fully endowed with flowers and leaves made of the seven treasures," yet it does not mention the matter of the wind playing celestial music; this was therefore taken from the *Shorter Version* (*Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā*) to form the present text on the visualization of the trees.

Therefore, that sutra says: "When a gentle breeze stirs the rows of various jeweled trees and the jeweled nets, they produce subtle and wondrous sounds, like hundreds of thousands of kinds of music performed simultaneously. Hence it is said: "They flourish together with celestial music."

Next, the ponds are shown; the Sūtra says: "There are eight ponds of water produced from the King of Wish-fulfilling Jewels, divided into fourteen branches with channels of gold, wherein the flow of mani-jewels pours down among the flowers."

Its sound is subtle and wondrous, expounding upon suffering, emptiness, impermanence, non-self, the various pāramitās, and so forth; therefore, it is said that "it harmonizes its resonance with the sūtras."
2. From "Contemplating the Flesh" (*guān ròu*) below, the primary retribution (*zhèngbào*) is shown.

First, the contemplations of the two Bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta are clarified, because both of these contemplations clarify the fleshly protuberance on the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*).

The Sūtra states: "If there are those who wish to contemplate Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, they should first contemplate the *uṣṇīṣa* on his crown, then the celestial crown, and finally the other various marks."
"One should also contemplate them in sequence.
Regarding Śrīkṣetra, the Sūtra says: "The uṣṇīṣa on his crown is like a padma flower; atop this uṣṇīṣa is a jeweled vase filled with various radiances, universally manifesting the Buddha-activities."
"The remaining bodily characteristics are no different from those of Avalokiteśvara and the others.
This is the essential method for practitioners to contemplate the two Great Beings as taught by the Tathāgata.
These two bodhisattvas are next in line for the position of successor; as they now serve as close attendants, they are called "those who gaze upon and attend.

Next, the visualization of Amitābha is shown; the sutra says: "One who contemplates the Buddha of Immeasurable Life enters through a single mark and excellence, contemplating only the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows until it is extremely clear."
"Those who see the white tuft between the eyebrows will naturally have the eighty-four thousand marks manifest"—is this not an instruction on the gateway to the method of contemplation?
Therefore, it is said: "By recollecting the mark of the tuft, one beholds the Tathāgata."
3. Regarding the section beginning with "And as for," it demonstrates the contemplations of the three grades.
The sub-commentary below judges this, stating: "There are two intentions in contemplating the three grades of rebirth:

first, to cause [practitioners] to abandon the middle and lower grades and cultivate the upper grade; second, to cause them to recognize the hierarchy of stages, which corresponds to the three grades of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*."
Regarding these two intentions, the first encourages one's own practice while the second concerns observing others; therefore, they are briefly described here.

As for encouraging one's own practice, the merit of the practitioner cultivating contemplation varies in depth, resulting in three grades of signs of rebirth; thus it is said, "When their eyes close and life ends," and so forth.

The first section clarifies the highest grade of the highest birth and the highest grade of the middle birth; because the sutra explains that those of the highest birth ride upon a vajra platform while those of the middle birth sit upon a purple-gold platform, it refers to them as "exalted precious platforms."
Next, following the passage "The Text is Accomplished," the lower birth of the highest grade is explained.
The Sūtra states: "One immediately sees oneself sitting upon a golden lotus flower. Regarding the phrase "the impression is formed and the seal is destroyed":

the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 27, says, "It is like a wax seal pressed into clay; as the seal and the clay meet, the seal vanishes and the impression is formed. This is used as a metaphor for how the present aggregates (*skandhas*) of an ordinary person cease and the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) aggregates arise. Here, this text is borrowed to illustrate how the aggregates of a reborn Bodhisattva cease in this land and their aggregates arise in that land.
One should know that when one is on the verge of death, seeing oneself seated upon a golden lotus is because one has already formed the *antarābhava* (intermediate state) for rebirth in that land.

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* clarifies that those of extreme goodness or extreme evil do not pass through the intermediate state, just as a spear thrown by hand does not leave the hand before it reaches its mark.
Although there are three grades among the superior class, they all belong to the highest category.
Next, the text generally indicates that those who attain birth in the three grades alike transcend the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*).

Regarding the phrase "according to the three grades," this does not mean following others; rather, it refers to following what one has cultivated oneself. The karmic practices of all three grades are capable of cutting across the five paths of existence horizontally, ensuring eternal non-retrogression.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "Those who are reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang) will cross transversely over the five evil paths.

Regarding the "five sufferings," in this world, beings in all five realms of existence cannot escape suffering; for even though those in the heavenly realm enjoy pleasure, they eventually fall back into the evil destinies.
2. From "May be called" (*kewei*) onwards, there is a concluding eulogy of the contemplative practice (*guanxing*).
"Subtle conduct" (*weixing*) refers to the praise that although the three types of karma pertain to body and speech, they are the goodness of their operational movement.
Now, practicing in accordance with principle, all constitute the practice of non-action (*anabhisamskāra*), which is profound, subtle, and signless.
"Sublime Contemplation" refers to the praise of the sixteen contemplations.

Although they rely upon the environment and inhabitants of the Pure Land, they are all contemplated as being in accord with the nature of reality, beyond all relational dependence; this is precisely the inconceivable, perfect, and sublime contemplation.

This contemplative practice enables the practitioner to reach the four pure lands; even while still possessing the afflictions of views and thoughts, one is able to avoid regression. It is truly the ultimate path and the most subtle and essential art.
Thus, having expressed this summary of my intent, I hope that those who hear it will revere and practice it.

How tragic, how tragic, that there are those of inferior character who treat birth and death with contempt and deceit, who do not seek non-retrogression, and who give rise to slander against this essential method, thereby obstructing others!
2. From "This Sūtra" onwards, the essential body of the sūtra is described.

Regarding "contemplation of the mind": while the sūtra takes the contemplation of the Buddha as its title, the commentary now takes the contemplation of the mind as its essence; these two are not different, for only this constitutes the present contemplation.

This is because the perfect understanding is entirely different from that of the Hīnayāna; the latter is ignorant of "mind-only" and perceives the Buddha as existing externally, and thus the essence of mind and Buddha are considered distinct.
A practitioner of the Mahāyāna knows that their own single mind possesses the nature of all Buddhas, and by relying on objects to cultivate contemplation, the marks of the Buddha become manifest.
Now, observing that the environment and inhabitants of Amitābha serve as conditions to permeate the nature of the mind,
the environment and inhabitants of Ultimate Bliss possessed within the nature of the mind arise through this permeation.
Since they arise from what is already possessed by the mind, how could they be separate from the nature of the mind?

The entire mind is the Buddha, and the entire Buddha is the mind; throughout the day one contemplates the mind and throughout the day one contemplates the Buddha. Therefore, although the wording differs between the *Jingmu* and the *Lizong*, their meaning is no different.

Furthermore, one must understand this: if one contemplates the Buddha, one must necessarily illumine the mind; however, if one focuses exclusively on the mind, it does not necessarily involve relying upon the Buddha. For example, in the *Ekākṣara-samādhi*, one directly contemplates a single thought-moment without relying on another Buddha as the object of focus.

Whether it be the Pratyutpanna Samādhi or this method of contemplation, one begins by contemplating the environment and the beings of Sukhāvatī; yet, since this contemplation of the environment and beings is not separate from the nature of the mind, it is called "contemplation of the mind."

One should know that this contemplation does not focus exclusively on the mind; when divided into internal and external aspects, this belongs to external contemplation, as it is based upon the contemplation of the Buddha’s body and its environment (the *āśraya* and *sambhoga*).
Therefore, the title of the sutra is called "Contemplating the Buddha."
Regarding the difficulty or ease [of practice], one must now follow the easier path.
The *Fahua xuanyi* states: "The Buddha-dharma is too lofty and sentient beings are too numerous; thus, it is difficult for those at the initial stage."
"Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction; thus, contemplating the mind is easy.

This present method of contemplation does not merely involve contemplating the Buddha; rather, it relies on the contemplation of the mind to manifest the sublime by means of the base. Therefore, although one practices the contemplation of the Buddha, it is not called difficult.

Thus we know that this present sutra takes mental contemplation as its primary tenet, with the aim of perceiving the Buddha; therefore, these two explanations do not diverge in their essential meaning.

Furthermore, one should understand that the inconceivable essence of the perfectly interfused Dharma-realm constitutes my single thought-moment, and likewise, it constitutes the entirety of sentient beings and Buddhas, the environment and the enlightened ones, the faculties and the objects. From a single mind to a single speck of dust, down to a single atom, there is nothing that is not the entire body of the Dharma-realm manifesting itself.
Since each and every phenomenon functions as the entirety of the dharma-realm, to take up even one is to encompass the full extent of the perfectly interfused dharma-realm.
Since it is the entire dharma-realm, what single thing could there be that does not possess all phenomena?

As a biased commentator in the *Yili* says: "Among the four teachings, only in the Perfect Teaching (yuan) is it discussed that the mind possesses all dharmas; as for the physical form, color, and the environment of dependent retribution, their possession is not discussed."
"Only through the single, sudden teaching can it be clarified that all three locations are fully endowed with all dharmas.
Master Jingxi’s commentary states: "Within the four teachings, how could the Perfect Teaching ever fail to say that the dharmas are fully present in all three locations?"

Those who profess our present school, if they claim that the mind possesses form and other phenomena but does not possess [the principle of] non-possession, are sharing in the same erroneous view of establishing a gradual perfection; compared to that, our suddenness is as vastly different as heaven and earth, yet we are still inferior to them—how could such a position even be considered part of our present school?
Since every single phenomenon (dharma) possesses all phenomena within it, our school establishes the principle that there is "only form" or "only fragrance," and so forth.
If this is the case, why do the sutras and treatises generally establish the mind alone as the universal object of contemplation for all phenomena?

This is because if one contemplates such objects as ordinary beings and Buddhas, their phenomena are separated and distinct, making it difficult to forget the distinction between the subject and the object.
Contemplating the mind-dharma is both proximate and essential; since it is that which creates [all things], its meaning is easily manifested.
Furthermore, that which is the observer itself becomes the object of illumination, because it is easy to sever discursive thought.
The *Miaoxuan* states: "The three [truths] are without distinction; when one contemplates the mind, it is easy."
"Even when surveying other realms, one must likewise rely upon the mind.
This sutra precisely prescribes contemplating the Buddha by relying upon the mind.

Regarding "taking the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as the essence," it is only through the central tenet of contemplating with the mind that the profound and vast essence of the Middle Way’s true reality can be manifested.

Why is this so? If one contemplates the Buddha as being external to the mind, even if one is able to employ reasoning, one will see only the partial truth; this is just like Śāriputra, who contemplated the Buddha’s Dharma-body and realized only the limited principle of the Lesser Vehicle.

Now, based on the principle of "mind-only," one contemplates the Buddha’s environment and its inhabitants to manifest the essence of the Middle and Reality; since the Middle must necessarily illuminate the Three Truths simultaneously and in their entirety, it is said that "this sutra takes mental contemplation as its school and the true aspect (bhūtalakṣaṇa) as its essence"—the text specifically emphasizes this point.
To present the essence of the school is to establish the preceding exposition on contemplation and reveal the subsequent exposition of the title.

Regarding the establishment of the former: although the text of the exposition on contemplation contains the principles of the three contemplations and four lands, its language is general and concise; thus, there is a fear that those who lose the intended meaning might think it merely expounds the intent of the contemplative practice for the Pure Land of Co-residence.

Having completed the introduction to the contemplation, he specifically reveals the essence of the wondrous contemplation of "mind-only" in order to manifest the substance of the Middle Way’s true reality (*bhūtatathatā*).

Since true reality is itself the land of eternal, quiescent light, how could it be possible to manifest this quiescent light of true reality by claiming that the sixteen contemplations merely observe the marks of the responsive Buddhas and their environments?

If, by employing the three contemplations in their perfected form within these sixteen [practices], one can still attain the ultimate bliss of the *śāntaprabhāsa* (calm-light) realm, how much more so could one not attain the ultimate bliss of the three lands?
By this, the preceding textual meanings concerning the Land of Bliss, its golden treasures, and so forth, all clarify the causes and effects of the four kinds of pure lands.

Regarding the manifestation of the latter: if a practitioner grasps the essential meaning of this school, they will understand that the title’s description of the Buddha who speaks, the assembly and environment of those for whom the contemplative object is taught, and the general name—all such meanings are perfectly sublime, neither small nor partial; only then does it truly constitute the title of the present sutra.
In the introduction to the title, it is said that between the two pillars lie the essence and the substance; this is where the intent resides.
Third, following the phrase "That which is spoken," the titles of the scripture are introduced in two parts:
first, the individual title.
These seven characters encompass both the speaker and the spoken, as well as the observer and the observed; the main text’s explanation of the title fully elucidates their meaning.
This preface, however, merely clarifies the intent behind establishing the title: that the superior subsumes the inferior and the particular is gathered into the general.
Because the realm of the Buddha is the most supreme among the sixteen realms, it is said that "the Buddha is the supreme object of contemplation.

Indeed, these sixteen contemplations do not transcend the distinction between the primary and secondary rewards (the environment and the inhabitants), as well as the host and the retinue. If we discuss the primary and secondary rewards, the Buddha represents the primary reward; by citing the primary, the secondary is subsumed, thereby encompassing the six contemplations of the sun, water, earth, trees, and so forth.

If we distinguish between the principal subject and the subjects under his guidance, the Buddha is the principal subject, while the description of the subjects encompasses the retinue; this includes the nine contemplations, such as those of Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the three grades of rebirth.
Therefore, it is said: "Although there are sixteen contemplations, by speaking of the Buddha, all are encompassed."

Therefore, entering the main text, the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) are explained as the subject that contemplates, and the wondrous Three Bodies (*trikāya*) are explained as the Buddha who is contemplated.
Since the Buddha already subsumes the remaining fifteen objects, are they not each and every one the perfect and wondrous Three Truths and Three Contemplations?
2. "The 'Sūtra'" below is the general title.
Regarding the commentaries on the Confucian Classics, there are two interpretations of this term:
because they serve as models for ten thousand generations, it is interpreted as "Law" (dharma); [and because they record the words of the sages, it is interpreted as "Record"].
The teachings of a hundred kings have not changed; thus, their instructions are constant.

Buddhist scriptures are likewise: they provide a model for all ten realms and remain unchanging throughout the three periods of time. Furthermore, one explains these scriptures by means of their underlying principles.
Because these are the teachings of self-realization proclaimed from the golden mouth of the Great Sage Buddha, they are called "Sūtras.
The *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra) provides a detailed explanation of this general name; students of this school must investigate it thoroughly.

First, discussing the general and specific [aspects] regarding the three locations, in three parts:
first, concerning a single transformation, in two parts:
first, the explanation; second... [etc.]
First, it is shown that all titles possess both general and specific aspects.

In the commentaries of others on sutra titles, they universally take the character "sutra" (jing) as the teaching that expresses (the *nirukta*), while all other characters are taken as the meanings expressed (the *lakṣya*).
To divide it in this manner is a grave departure from the Buddha’s intent.

Furthermore, since both the person and the dharma, as well as the analogy, are all merely names, they are surely the expressive designators (vācaka); how then can they be categorically assigned solely to the expressed meaning (vācya)?

The word "sūtra" cannot be unilaterally categorized as belonging solely to the category of teaching (*śāsana*). As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "The treasury of the *Dharmapada-sūtra* is profound, firm, remote, and deep; no one can reach it. It further says: "Being protected by the Buddhas, they plant the roots of virtue, enter the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), and give rise to the mind that seeks to save all sentient beings."
"By accomplishing four dharmas, one will certainly obtain this sutra.

The commentary explains that these four are the opening, showing, awakening to, and entering into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; realizing the principle through knowledge and vision is what is meant by "obtaining the sutra."
Are these two not, in fact, taking principle as the sūtra?
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states, "The Buddhas of the ten directions constantly keep this sūtra in mind. How could it be that the Buddhas merely keep the teaching in mind?
Such examples are numerous and cannot be cited in full.
Thus, we know that various masters who explain the titles of the various sutras by treating the designator as the designated have missed the essential meaning to an extreme degree.
Our school employs both the general and specific explanations for titles; only in this way is there no loss of the intended sense.
2. Below the section "General Principles," it is explained that there are three types of general and specific [teachings].
Herein, we clarify that both the names "general" and "specific" applied to various sutras are equally expressive (the signifier) and equally expressed (the signified).

This is because both the general and the specific each fully encompass the aspects of teaching (*śāsana*), practice (*pratipatti*), and principle (*naya*); do not assume that these two names refer only to the teaching.
One must understand that the general and the specific each possess their own names for teaching, practice, and principle.
Just as there is a separate title, the Buddha’s teaching is the contemplation, which is itself the practice;
Amitāyus Buddha is the principle. Is this not, then, a separate teaching, a separate practice, and a separate principle?
These three distinctions correspond to the words of the sūtra, namely: the universal teaching, the universal practice, and the universal principle.
Now, within these three, the first section clarifies the universality and particularity of the teaching, in two parts:
first, the formal clarification of the single transformation.

Regarding the general name: whether taught all at once or gradually, whether employing provisional means or revealing the ultimate, all works outside the Vinaya and Śāstra categories are termed "Sūtra"; thus, it is called "general.
Regarding the specific names: although particular designations are numerous, we shall now follow three types—namely, those based on persons, those based on dharmas, and those based on metaphors.
There are three single [teachings], three combined [teachings], and one complete [teaching], which together constitute seven distinct categories.
As for the three single [teachings]: the single person, such as in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* and others;
the single dharma, such as in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* and others.
A single analogy is found, for example, in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and others.
Regarding the threefold [analogy], there are those concerning persons and dharmas, such as in the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and others;
and those concerning dharmas and analogies, such as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and others.
The analogy for the person is found, for example, in the *Tathāgata-siṃhanāda-sūtra* and others.
The analogy that fully encompasses both the person and the dharma is found, for example, in the *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-ekayāna-mahā-upāya-parivarta-vipula-sūtra* and others.
By combining these seven specific [teachings] with the general [teaching], the entire body of the Buddha’s Dharma throughout his lifetime is indicated.
Second, from the phrase "this present sutra" onwards, the specific reference is made to this particular sutra.

Within the entirety of the Buddha’s single transformation (one-vehicle teaching), the mention of "this sutra" is used to clarify the seven specific [teachings]; since this belongs to the category of the "single person," it is so stated.
Although they belong to a single person, the person is naturally divided: one can speak of Śākyamuni and that which was spoken by Amitābha; thus, these two individuals serve as distinct titles.
Since the sūtra represents a single transformation, it is called the "common name."

Since the character "guān" (contemplation) is present, it should logically encompass both person and dharma; however, because the person is subsumed within the object of contemplation, it is omitted here for brevity.
Nevertheless, as this is a partial explanation of the common and distinct aspects rather than a comprehensive exposition, it is not yet fully detailed.
2. Regarding the section beginning with "As for practice" (*wei xing*), it concerns both general and specific practices.
In various sutras, there are instances where a single type of practice is used as a specific name; when contrasted with a general name, that sutra then represents a general practice.
If one were to discuss individual practices, their number is immeasurable and difficult to exhaustively describe.
Now, by indicating them through increasing numerical categories for the sake of practitioners, they may be more easily understood:

first, such as the single practice; second, such as the two wisdoms; third, such as the three contemplations; fourth, such as the four foundations of mindfulness; fifth, such as the five faculties; sixth, such as the six subtle gates; seventh, such as the seven factors of enlightenment; eighth, such as the eightfold noble path; ninth, such as the nine meditations; tenth, such as the ten perfections—and so on, up to hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, billions, and an infinite number of practices.
These distinct practices all lead toward nirvana and its ultimate four virtues; briefly stated, these are permanence and bliss.
Since these distinct practices are, in terms of their convergence toward nirvana, universally applicable, they constitute the *Xingjing* (Sutra of Practice).

In that *Śāstra-vyākhyā*, the general and specific aspects of practice are distinguished by means of cause and fruit; however, one must understand that its intent does not mean the practice only becomes "general" upon reaching the fruit.
To understand this intent: based on the individual cultivation of causes, it is called "specific practice";
yet, in terms of tending toward a single fruit, this very specificity is itself "general."
This is a case where the discourse on the general [teaching] is applied to the specific occasion, and the discourse on the specific occasion is applied to the general time.
This applies not only to practice but also to doctrine and principle.

For example, regarding the correspondence between the capacities of beings and the general or specific aspects of the teaching: "The Buddha preaches the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each understand it according to their own kind."

Individual understanding constitutes the distinction of capacities, while the single sound constitutes the universality of the response; individual understanding does not depart from the single sound, and the single sound does not obstruct individual understanding.

As stated in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra-śāstra*, that which expresses through words is the universal teaching (*sāmānya-dharma*), while the reason why it is so expressed is the specific teaching (*viśeṣa-dharma*). This "reason" refers precisely to the four *satyana* (fourfold methods of conversion); each *satyana* employs words, and each word does not depart from the *satyana*.

Just as names and realities correspond to principles through both the general and the particular—where multiple names do not depart from a single reality, and a single reality does not preclude multiple names—the three aspects of the general and the particular are all simultaneous.

All these resemble the melodic tones of wind instruments within music: they are general with respect to sound, yet distinct with respect to the musical pieces; thus, the two functions—general and distinct—do not obstruct one another.
Third, regarding the phrase "Although in principle," etc., this concerns the general and distinct aspects of principle.

Name and reality correspond to one another; the name is itself the gate, whereby four gates manifest a single principle. This is also a case where particular phenomena correspond to the universal principle.
This is because various sutras frequently use a single phenomenon to manifest the principle, thereby attaining distinct names for that principle.
Regarding such a sutra title, the name of Amitāyus Buddha serves as the specific principle (*bieli*), while the generic term "sutra" serves as the general principle (*tongli*).

If one seeks to interpret the title of a sutra through both general and specific principles within a single dispensation (*yihua*), nothing is more suitable than employing the four gates as the specific principle.
Regarding the four gates—the gate of existence, the gate of emptiness, the gate of both, and the gate of neither—their names apply generally across all teachings.
However, one must distinguish them according to the four teachings, namely: the Tripitaka Teaching, the Shared Teaching, the Distinct Teaching, and the Perfect Teaching.
Each of the four teachings opens up four gates—“existence” and so forth; thus, the four sets of four constitute sixteen gates. These expound the distinct principles, resulting in sixteen principles.
Yet, if even the principles are not one, how could there be sixteen?

However, the principle of non-obstruction can respond to all gateways; it is like space, whose essence is truly neither square nor round, neither large nor small. Because it is unobstructed, it can manifest infinite forms according to objects such as those that are square or round.
Speaking from the perspective of the immeasurable, this refers to the specific principle;
as for their essence being the single emptiness, it is called the universal principle.
There is no universality without particularity, and no particularity without universality; the union of the universal and the particular establishes the title of this work.
Second, the section beginning with "This refers to" concludes that within each of the five periods, every sutra title possesses both a general and a specific aspect.
If one does not employ this method of judging through teaching, practice, and principle, then to merely distinguish between the general and the specific is entirely without basis.

Nevertheless, immeasurable practices converge upon the single reality of permanence and bliss; the four teachings and four gates equally expound this one principle. If one is exclusively devoted to the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtras) yet is not yet capable of hearing this, it would be to prematurely grasp the intent of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and speak across the stages [of the teaching].
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if one were to explain the various sūtras without relying on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, how could one possibly exhaust the full scope of his single transformation?
Second, under the heading “Furthermore, by means of,” the text relies upon a single title.

The titles of the various *Ekottarika-āgama* (One-Transformation) scriptures comprise both general and specific names, as well as the three aspects of teaching and so forth; since their scope is so vast, reflection and cultivation may be difficult. Therefore, by means of the very title of the scripture currently being explained, the teaching, practice, and principle can be clearly seen in their entirety.

These three are distinct; yet, when contrasted with the words of the sutra, they constitute the threefold penetration. Therefore, it is said that "there is both a general and a specific meaning according to the spontaneous [nature of the text].

This is intended to enable the practitioner, through this single title alone, to engage in the exposition of the teachings, to initiate the practice of contemplation, and to perceive the true principle of the Buddha.
3. Regarding the section "Furthermore, with respect to" below, it concerns a single character.
Although the title involves three names, by now demonstrating this one character, the three aspects of understanding, practice, and realization are all fully encompassed.
This further divides into two parts:
first, an explanation that incorporates both the words and their meaning as presented in the title.

The word "expounded" (*shuo*) in the title is most capable of manifesting the teaching, the practice, and the principle; therefore, the passage from the *Śāstra*, "that which is practiced is as that which is expounded," is cited to demonstrate that practice and principle are contained within the act of expounding.
"Tathatā" (Suchness) refers to True Suchness (*bhūtatathatā*).
"Tathā" (Thus) means non-differentiation.

Within the single nature of true awakening, all phenomena are without distinction and equal throughout the three periods of time; only by accords with this principle of suchness can one ensure that what is expressed by mind and speech does not differ from one's practice.

Therefore, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* says: "How does one expound the Dharma for others? It is by remaining unmoving in suchness (*tathatā*). And the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says: "The emptiness of all phenomena is the seat; sitting upon this, one preaches the Dharma."
Understanding "sameness" through phenomena means that two things are similar and thus considered non-different.
Understanding "sameness" through principle means that the natures of the two things are one; only then can they be called non-different.
Therefore, the explanation of the sūtras is as follows.
In the Tripiṭaka, one transmits what the Buddha taught, like water being poured from one vessel into another; this is called "the letter as such" (wénrú).
The Mahāyāna teachings are not thus; they universally take the mutual identity of the two truths to be "as such" (rú).
Specifically, the Separate Teaching regards only the Middle Way as suchness;
the Perfect Teaching regards the nature of words being detached from [inherent existence] as suchness.
It is with reference to these three teachings that one speaks of "the suchness of words."

In this treatise, when considering the principle through contemplation, mind and speech are one in principle; only then can one speak and practice such that they accord with *tathatā* (suchness) without difference.
This ensures that the speaker’s practice accords with the principle of suchness.
Second, from the phrase "The Buddha is... onwards, the explanation proceeds by means of the mutual inclusion of all characters.
The Buddha is the fundamental source and the ultimate awakened essence; being neither quiescent nor illuminating, he belongs to the Dharmakāya.
The character "contemplation" (guān) is pure wisdom, which is eternally illuminating while remaining quiescent; thus, it belongs to Prajñā.
Amitāyus represents sovereign spiritual power; it illuminates while remaining eternally quiescent, and thus belongs to liberation.
That the various characters are now divided and correlated with the three virtues is profoundly significant.

Why is this so? Previously, we clarified the principle of teaching and practice through a single character; although the meaning of that character was explained as being complete in all three aspects, since this was discussed in terms of cultivation, it still pertained generally to the preceding teachings, and furthermore, it had not yet clarified that every single character possesses these three.

Therefore, we now specifically employ the three virtues of *nirvāṇa* in relation to these characters to demonstrate that the nature of each character inherently possesses these three; this is beyond the capacity of those taught by previous teachings to conceive or describe.
This is because the nature of the three virtues is fundamentally perfect and harmonious, with each one mutually containing the others: the Dharma-body alone is not the Dharma-body;
the Dharma-body must necessarily possess Prajñā and Vimukti. Prajñā alone is not Prajñā;
Prajñā must necessarily possess Vimukti and the Dharma-body. Vimukti alone is not Vimukti; Vimukti must necessarily possess the Dharma-body and Prajñā.
The three virtues are precisely the triad of teaching, practice, and principle.
Prajñā is the teaching, because wisdom resides in the exposition;
Vimukti is practice, because its function arises from conditions.
The Dharma-body belongs to principle (*li*), as it is that which is manifested.
Since the character "Buddha" (*fo*) is the principle of the Dharma-body, it inherently possesses both the two virtues as well as the teaching and practice.
Since the character "Contemplation" (*guan*) belongs to the teaching of Prajñā, it likewise possesses both the two virtues as well as the practice and principle.
The Immeasurable Life (Amitāyus) is both the practice of liberation and possesses the two virtues as well as the principle and the teaching.
Were it not so, how could one attain the three by means of the one, or attain the one by means of the three?
Question:

Originally, it was held that a single character fully encompasses both teaching (jiao) and practice-and-principle (xingli). Now, why is it that only the three characters "Amitāyus" can fully embody these three [aspects]?
If so, it cannot be called an explanation based on a single character.
Answer:
To explain the various characters of the title in relation to the Three Virtues (triguṇa) is indeed a sublime discourse; its value lies in grasping the underlying meaning.

It is intended to enable practitioners to know that the nature of the Three Virtues pervades all places: whether it be a single character or phrase, a single verse or chapter, a single treatise or scripture, a single period or transformation—even down to all phenomena of the environment and its inhabitants, both form and mind—whether many they are the Three Virtues, and whether few they are the Three Virtues. A single mote of dust does not diminish the Three Virtues, nor does an ocean of lands enlarge them.
Therefore, it quotes the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, saying: "Within one, understand the immeasurable," and so forth.
If one grasps this meaning, then the wondrous contemplation of the present possesses the aspect of cultivation.

Since a single form of matter can illuminate the three bodies, and a single atom of the dependent retribution is itself the Land of Peaceful Light, all sixteen contemplations illuminate the three truths.
Those who do not believe this would be failing their Ancestor in establishing this Dharma.
2. From "At one" below, the comparison is made by means of a single character, in three parts:
first, the actual comparison.
This reaches upward to the sublime ultimate meaning, proceeding from the broad to the narrow;
Now, comparing their merits from the least to the greatest:
even a single word can expound the principle of the Great Nirvana, let alone the entirety of the sutras—how could they not be complete and universal?
Second, "Therefore, the sutra... and below, cites the sutra as proof.
As stated in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and various other Mahāyāna scriptures, this is frequently taught.
Third, from the words "If not" onwards, the conclusion regarding what is attained now is presented.

If it were not clarified that even a single character fully embodies the three virtues (*triguṇa*), then the immeasurable and boundless merit of upholding even a single phrase or a single title as taught in the various sūtras would become a mere empty fabrication.
Were it not for having entered samādhi and attained the revolving dhāraṇī at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), how could one possibly possess such wondrous and sovereign eloquence?
Second, from "The Initial Explanation" onwards, the specific [teachings] are explained in detail; this sets aside the general explanation to clarify the particular.
Section Four:
The Explanation of the Text. Part One: Explaining the Character "Buddha" (in two sections).
Part One: Directly correlating the name "Buddha" with the six stages of realization (in two sections).
First, the title is translated and indicated.
In Sanskrit it is called *buddha*, which in the language of China means "the Awakened One" (*jùézhě*); this refers to the Teacher who expounds the doctrine.
His specific epithet is Śākyamuni; there are ten general titles, and here the ninth is cited, hence he is designated as "Buddha."
Since it is the ultimate fruit, it is the consummate awakening.
The *Awakening of Faith* states: "When the mind first arises, the mind has no initial characteristic, for it is far removed from even subtle thoughts."
"The mind is itself eternally abiding; this is called ultimate awakening.

This awakening is perfectly pure and free from all opposition; it integrates and subsumes the Buddhas and sentient beings, as well as their environments and inhabitants, such that the ten directions and three periods of time penetrate one another without limit. The five stages of dwelling and two types of death are completely purified without remainder; it is immeasurably profound and forever beyond the reach of thought or speculation, yet is conventionally termed "Sublime Awakening."
This meaning of "awakening" (*jue*) has six aspects; "aspect" (*ji*) here refers to its categories.
Now, the awakening of Śākyamuni is ultimately the perfect and pure awakening.

All ordinary beings and sages are entirely this awakening in their totality; yet, although they are entirely it, the characteristics of delusion and enlightenment, as well as cause and effect, differ. Therefore, one distinguishes this awakening through six aspects: namely, the aspect of principle (*li*), the aspect of names and words (*mingzi*), the aspect of contemplative practice (*guanxing*), the aspect of semblance (*xiangsi*), the aspect of partial realization (*fenzheng*), and the aspect of ultimate perfection (*jiuzhong*).

However, if one does not know that nature is defiled and nature is evil, then all existing defilement and evil must necessarily be severed and destroyed; how then could one argue that the whole is inherently perverse?
Because it is the whole, one avoids despondency;
because there are six types of discrimination, one avoids overweening pride.

The six [phenomena] are not separate from the "suchness" (ji), and suchness does not obstruct the six; thus, the principle of the "sixfold suchness" (liu ji) is established, and the stages of the Perfect Teaching (yuan wei) can be discerned.
Question:
When it is said that the entire substance of ordinary beings and sages is identical with the Buddha, does this mean they are identical with the Buddha who is their own future fruition?
Is this the already perfected Buddha Śākyamuni?
Answer:

The body of the two Buddhas—the one who shall be the fruit in the future and the one who has already become Śākyamuni—is ultimately not distinct; therefore, all Buddhas of fruition are Buddhas of the nature of birth.

When deluded, they are deluded together; when seeing, they see together. Therefore, regarding both oneself and others, as well as the Buddhas, one may now discern the meaning of the "six stages of identity" (*liujie*) within their physical and mental faculties.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the principle of the six identities does not apply exclusively to Buddhas. For all beings—whether provisional or real, belonging to the Three Vehicles, humans, or devas, and even down to dung beetles and those in the hells—one must discern their beginning and end through these six stages. That is to say: there is the dung beetle of principle (*li*), the dung beetle of name (*mingzi*), and so on, up to the ultimate dung beetle (*jiujing*).
Now, as this is the teaching of the Buddha, we shall discuss it from the perspective of the Buddha; for the treatise holds that all ten realms are the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
There is nothing that is not the *dharmadhātu*, and each remains unchanged; thus, when the names are removed, it does not reveal only the Buddha, but the other nine realms are likewise manifested.
As for the attainment of the fruit, all ten [stages] reach ultimate perfection; thus, even creatures such as dung beetles are clearly explained through the six stages of "immediacy.
Second, from the section on "Nirvāṇa" onwards, the awakening is extensively elucidated in six parts:
first, the stage of "principle-immediacy" (*li-ji*).

These six kinds are all names for the meaning that phenomena and principle are non-dual in essence; yet among phenomena there are both adverse and favorable aspects. The five—namely, names and so forth—are favorable practices of phenomena, whereas the single nature-reality is purely an adverse practice of phenomena.
These matters of opposition and conformity are non-dual with the fundamental principle of original enlightenment; from what source, then, could the names "opposition" and "conformity" be established?
Because one knows their non-duality, all phenomena accord with the principle, and thus they are termed "conformity."
Those who do not understand act in ways that all contradict principle; therefore, these are called "rebellious.
As for the five [categories] beginning with names, whether shallow or deep, they are all known and all accordant [with principle].

If, at the initial stage of principle, there is only delusion and only opposition, yet the matters of delusion and opposition have never for a moment deviated from the awakened principle, it is therefore called "being Buddha. Why is this so?
This is because the nature of sentient beings inherently possesses defilement and evil that cannot be altered; yet this nature is perfectly luminous and thus is called "Buddha.
The inherent defilement and inherent evil manifest as the totality of all activity, and the cultivated defilement and cultivated evil possess no separate essence apart from them.
Since all cultivation is this very nature, one attains the Buddha who is non-different from principle even within deluded phenomena.

Yet, by means of this very principle, one gives rise to delusions and creates karma, cycling through birth and death, while remaining entirely unaware that phenomena are wholly identical to principle.
The principle that functions throughout long kalpas remains unknown throughout those long kalpas; yet, it is not because of this ignorance that the principle is not the Buddha.
Because it is entirely identical [to the Buddha], the principle is itself the Buddha; however, because it is characterized by ignorance, it does not constitute the latter five identities.

However, "the principle itself is the Buddha" (li-ji fo) represents the most minimal level of designation; this is because it utterly lacks the realization of understanding, practice, and verification, and consists merely of the fact that the rational nature is inherently suchness.

Furthermore, "the principle itself is the Buddha" does not mean pointing to a principle outside of phenomena and designating that as the Buddha; rather, it means that the principle of the three obstructions is entirely the Buddha.

Furthermore, it should be understood that what is called "the Buddha as principle" (li-ji-fo) is not the same as what is called "the Buddha as obstacle" (zhang-ji-fo). While the latter five obstacles involve cultivated virtues, this particular stage consists solely of the nature of reality (xing-li).
Furthermore, the obstacles are themselves the Buddha; their names remain applicable because the latter five [disciples] all realized that the three obstacles are identical to the Buddha.
This is explained in three parts:
first, citing various sūtras to demonstrate this identity.
First, citing the "Kāśyapa Chapter" of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, it says: "Sentient beings are themselves the Buddha.
Why is this? Because if one were apart from sentient beings, one could not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
From the "Chapter on the Tathāgata-nature": "The term 'self' (ātman) is synonymous with the meaning of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
That all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature is precisely the meaning of 'self.
