If one cultivates the contemplation of the conventional (prajñapti), one can accomplish the Buddha-dharma and benefit sentient beings; thus, while contemplating emptiness as a skillful means for entering the Middle Way, one does not dwell in the realization of the wisdom of emptiness. One must sweep away all attachments to the delusions of the triple world so they become empty, and investigate the beginning and end of the causes and conditions of all phenomena. Seeing that the layers of afflictions of view and thought are as numerous as dust motes or grains of sand, one universally contemplates and universally studies with a heart of great compassion; this is called "knowing the illness."

To thoroughly master the analysis of the nature and characteristics of all phenomena through various gateways, and to be proficient in every corresponding antidote—this is called "knowing the medicine.

To discern the depth or shallowness of afflictions and the maturity or immaturity of the faculties, to move others with supernatural powers and proclaim the truth with wisdom and eloquence, and to provide what is appropriate for each according to the four *siddhāntas* so that all may obtain benefit—in this way, one administers the medicine and they will be willing to take it and practice.
All of this arises from realizing emptiness and being able to enter into these conventional designations; therefore, this contemplation is named "entering the conventional from emptiness.

As for the term "and so forth" (*ādi*): previously, one removed views and attachments by using emptiness to destroy the conventional; now, one dispels the [afflictions] as numerous as the sands of the Ganges by using the conventional to destroy emptiness.

Each of the contemplations on emptiness and the conventional has its own function of refutation; as these have remained equal from beginning to end until now, it is further called the "Contemplation of Equality.

Regarding the phrase "this contemplation" and so forth: according to the *Śāstra*, if one correlates the person of the bodhisattva with the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), this is the fruit of the conventional contemplation, situated at the stage of the ten practices (*daśaprayoga*).
Below "The Two Emptinesses," the third section is the Middle Way (Madhyamaka).
First, the dual heading:

regarding "first contemplating the emptiness of birth-and-death," this refers to the initial faith of an individual practitioner; now, they realize that the fundamental nature is the eternally abiding Buddha-nature of the Middle Way. Because it follows the path of teaching, it is termed "mere middle" (*butian zhong*); it is exclusively good and pure, and does not possess defilement or evil.

Although there is no defilement or evil, its nature is luminous intelligence; yet when forceful awareness suddenly arises, objective realms manifest. One discriminates the characteristics of these objects and clings to "self" and "others. This non-deluded knowing, along with perverse thoughts and perverse views, manifests as present defilement and evil. Since these are not inherently possessed by the nature, they all exist as transformations produced through following conditions.

Because these are fabricated, they are not the primordial nature; therefore, view and thought are not identical with the Middle Way. Since they must necessarily be shattered, the sense of "identity" is not established, and thus one cannot say that there is only craving, only views, only form, or only fragrance.
If one wishes to cultivate the Middle Way, because the subject and object remain uninterrupted, the cultivation of emptiness is primary while the Middle View is secondary.
Why is this? Since the mind has already become attached to existence, one must specifically take emptiness as the object of focus to shatter these cravings and views.

The emptiness that is the object of contemplation belongs to the Dharma of the Two Vehicles; since it is not intrinsically possessed but must be cultivated separately, this emptiness is not ultimate. Therefore, the contemplation of emptiness merely empties birth and death.

Regarding "next, contemplate emptiness and nirvana": although the existence of birth-and-death has already been eliminated, the mind may still cling to emptiness; one must therefore employ a distinct object of focus on the conventional to break this attachment to emptiness.

If these are established as the dharmas of a bodhisattva, because they are not inherently possessed, they must also be cultivated separately; thus, one can sweep away attachment to emptiness by abiding in the emptiness of *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the phrase "this" and so forth: previously, one emptied *saṃsāra*, whereby the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *kleśa-kleśa*) were forgotten;
subsequently, one emptied *nirvāṇa*, whereby the delusions of the *pāṃśu-saṃkhyeya* (dust-like) category were exhausted.
Since the two delusions have been exhausted and the mind is free from partial attachment, this constitutes the "expedient means of dual negation.

Regarding the phrase "initial contemplation" and so forth: because one subsequently employs the two contemplations in sequence to contemplate the two truths, this constitutes the "expedient means of dual illumination."

Once the provisional means have been established, the perfect contemplation (*pariniṣpanna-vipaśyanā*) can be cultivated; within the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-praṇidhāna*), one takes the Middle Way Buddha-nature that has been revealed as the contemplation of the Middle Way. One observes with clarity that delusion and wisdom are non-dual and identical, and that the three contemplations are perfectly interfused—this is the practice of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Thus, one naturally enters into omniscience (*sarvajñā*).
The fruit of this contemplation is called the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), and its stage is the First Ground (*prathamabhūmi*).
Second is the threefold contemplation within a single mind.
This is a contemplation that accords with the nature of reality and an illumination that transcends all dualistic dependencies.

In essence, the nature of all phenomena is the Dharmakāya, Prajñā, and Vimukti, like the three dots of the letter *I*. These three are not isolated; each one is perfectly complete, such that to mention one is to include all three. Thus, these three virtues constitute the Three Truths: Prajñā is the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*), Vimukti is the Conventional Truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and the Dharmakāya is the Middle Truth (*madhyama-satya*).
Since virtue is neither vertical nor horizontal, and the Truth (satya) transcends both thought and discourse, this is the Truth realized by the Buddha.
Now, taking this Truth as the object of contemplation: since the Truth is simultaneously one and three, how could contemplation illuminate it sequentially?
Therefore, one establishes the gates of contemplation based on the wondrous truths, practicing the three contemplations within a single mind.

This contemplation is such that both subject and object are simultaneously transcended; how much more so for Amitāyus Buddha, who originally cultivated this contemplation and thereby achieved the three bodies (*trikāya*), wherein the Dharma-body and Reward-body merge and the True and Responsive bodies are fused. Were it not for this wondrous contemplation, how could the wondrous body be revealed?
If the master of transformation is such, his retinue is likewise so; since their primary retribution (*vipāka*) is already sublime, how could their secondary environment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) be coarse?
Therefore, all sixteen objects must be contemplated with sublime visualization.
This text is divided into three parts:
First, the explanation based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, in two parts:
first, the explanation of the characteristics, in two parts:
first, the explanation by way of the dharmas.

The three knowledges are those previously explained in sequence—the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). For the sake of easier understanding, they are here assigned respectively to three types of persons.
According to the *Kengyo Enron* (The Perfect Theory of Instantaneous Enlightenment), the three wisdoms are realized as a single reality within one mind.
The three wisdoms are the fruit, and the three contemplations are the cause; since the fruit resides in one mind, how could the causes be sequential?
Only when cause and effect are non-dual can one speak of "perfect cultivation"; therefore, immediately after presenting wisdom, the three contemplations are elucidated.

Regarding the phrase "a single contemplation is itself the three contemplations": this means that by taking up even a single contemplation, all three are fully present. For instance, if one takes up the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), then the provisional (*prajñapti*) and the middle (*madhyama*) are also empty; for all three contemplations are capable of sweeping away attachment to characteristics.
If one takes up the contemplation of the provisional (jia-guan), then emptiness and the middle are also provisional, because all three contemplations possess the principle of establishing dharmas.

If one takes up the contemplation of the middle (zhong-guan), then emptiness and the provisional are also the middle, because each respective locus of the three contemplations is free from all dependencies.
If one knows that the three contemplations reside solely within a single mind, then each individual contemplation spontaneously possesses all three.

Regarding "contemplating the One Truth as the Three Truths": while the names of the truths and the contemplations differ, their essence is not distinct; the truths give rise to the contemplations in their entirety, and the contemplations in turn illuminate the truths.
Since there is no separate essence, for what reason are the truths (satya) established and the contemplations (vipaśyanā) established?
If one wishes to differentiate them, they are explained according to three causes: the three natures constitute the truths, and the three practices constitute the contemplations.
The nature of ultimate realization is the True, while the nature of conditions is the Conventional; this very [nature] is the Middle Truth.
It is not that the cause of realization is not the Great Ultimate Truth; the same applies to the Conventional.
These three truths are precisely non-different in essence from the three contemplations.
To take stubborn emptiness as the truth and regard it as distinct from the essence of contemplation is likewise the case within the conventional realm.
As for the mutual inclusion of the three contemplations, it is because the three natures are fundamentally fused; this refers to the realization that the entirety of nature constitutes cultivation.
Second, from "The analogy is as follows" onwards, the argument is explained by means of an analogy.
One takes conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) as an analogy for the nature of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

A single moment of mind arises and immediately ceases; the interval between these two is called "abiding. Thus, although the three characteristics are not absent, they exist within a single moment of mind.

Even the three marks of impermanence reside within a fleeting thought; the three contemplations accord with the nature of reality, being unconditioned and unborn. Since these are fully present within a single mind, how could their meaning be at variance?
Second, from "This contemplation" onwards, the result is established.

Not understanding the fruits of wisdom and observing that all phenomena have no refuge, he demonstrates that through the perfection of contemplation, delusion is extinguished and principle is revealed; thus, he attains a sudden and wondrous realization that the three kinds of wisdom are substantially one within the single mind.

Alternatively, while the treatise fully discusses the three types of knowledge, it refers to them simply as "knowledge of all aspects" (*sarvākārajñatā*) when speaking from the perspective of their preeminence.
Regarding the term "quiescence" (*śānta*) and so forth, the treatise provides its own explanation.

The wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is characterized by the simultaneous quiescence of the two extremes of ignorance and the simultaneous illumination of the various categories of the two truths. Beginning from the first thought-moment, one perfectly cultivates the three contemplations; within this wondrous contemplation of the Middle Way, one simultaneously forgets both extremes in every thought-moment while simultaneously illuminating them in every thought-moment. This is the natural law of the single mind and its two contemplations.

Now, entering the stage of partial realization (*praveśa-bhūta-tattva*), the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is manifested; this is entirely due to the merit of the initial practices of forgetting and illuminating.
Second, citing the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* as proof:

the treatise states, "Of those phenomena produced through causes and conditions, I say they are empty; they are also called provisional designations, and they are also called the meaning of the Middle Way. This treatise encompasses all three vehicles.
Now, having realized the perfect contemplation (*yuan guan*), how could the phenomena confronted by this contemplation not arise from causes and conditions?

When practicing the perfect contemplation now, one must first understand and know that both the productive causes and conditions and the phenomena produced are inconceivable; only then can one contemplate emptiness, the provisional, and the middle within this realm.

Furthermore, one must clearly understand that the wondrous truth and the wondrous contemplation are both the subject of contemplation (*能觀*), while the aggregates (*skandha*) and other objects produced by causes and conditions are all the objects of contemplation (*所觀*).

Previously, it was stated directly that one contemplates a single truth through the three contemplations; however, one must know that this refers to contemplating the single truth and so forth within the context of the aggregates and other such objects.
Do not cling merely to the literal text; you must seek out and contemplate its meaning.

Furthermore, one cannot claim that because the inconceivable object of contemplation has already been understood, one may therefore no longer speak of the aggregates (*skandha*) and ignorance (*avidyā*).

Why is this? It was originally taught that causes and conditions, as well as the phenomena produced from them, are inconceivable. If it were not ignorance, what could be called "causes and conditions"?
If it were not the aggregates and so forth, what could be called "produced phenomena"?
Someone, seeing that the Dharma of the mind is subtle and wondrous, said: "The Dharma of the mind pertains to the cause and is explained in terms of delusion;
the Buddha-Dharma pertains to the fruit and is explained in terms of awakening. He then immediately raised an objection, saying:
"If the Dharma of the mind is called subtle and wondrous, how can it be delusion?"
It is precisely because this person does not understand the underlying principle.

To resolve delusion is the wondrous method; such a person is called "one of perfect realization. As the treatise explains that suffering and its origin are termed "unconditioned" (*anabhisaṃskāra*), and the twelve links of dependent origination are termed "inconceivable" (*acintya*), how could one not say that ignorance is also inconceivable?

Although a person understands that the essence of the wondrous Dharma is [the truth], they remain deluded; they do not realize that while the principle (li) is entirely within delusion, wondrous awakening (miaojue) is entirely comprised of understanding, and the four intermediate stages consist of both delusion and understanding coexisting.
If one does not contemplate delusion regarding the person who possesses a name, where would contemplation be applied?
If the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samanvāgama) does not shatter delusion, how could one ascend to Sublime Enlightenment (Samyaksaṃbodhi)?
To sever the lowest grade of afflictions with the highest grade of wisdom—is that affliction not delusion?
The manifold deviations of human beings are indeed numerous in their varieties.
The three types of wisdom as explained in the *Śāstra* have already been elucidated above.
Third, from "This contemplation" onwards, the conclusion is presented by way of the Subtle [Wisdom].
The first line offers a general praise for its subtle and wondrous nature.
The subsequent two lines praise its wonder by means of the "three-in-one" principle:

the one is not fixed as one, yet the one is precisely the three; the three are not fixed as three, yet the three are precisely the one. The *Śāstra* explains that this lack of fixity constitutes the inconceivable.
The next three phrases correspond to the sixteen [aspects] to praise their wondrousness.
The preceding clarification of the fusion of the one and the three constitutes the "single wondrous contemplation" in its totality.
This single contemplation pervades all gates; it is called "the one contemplation as all contemplations."
Although one enters through various gates, there is but a single wondrous contemplation, called "contemplating all as one contemplation.
If the contemplation is fixed upon one, do not enter many gates;
if the contemplation is fixed upon many, it cannot be made one.
In reality, this cannot be conceived through either unity or multiplicity; therefore, it is said to be "neither one nor all.
The final two lines provide a concluding demonstration:
although it is neither one nor many, it is capable of encompassing all things; thus, these sixteen [aspects] are none other than wondrous contemplation.
Fourth, the explanation of "Immeasurable Life" (Amitāyus) correctly demonstrates the object of contemplation for the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).

While the preceding section on the three contemplations provisionally took the three virtues and the three causes as the objects of truth (*satya-viṣaya*), this serves to demonstrate that the object of contemplation is a fusion and identity, thereby revealing the supreme excellence of the contemplating subject.

One must know that the three virtues within the nature are, in essence, the three bodies of all Buddhas; these very three virtues and three bodies constitute my own one mind and the three contemplations.

If it were otherwise, then one would perceive the Buddha as existing externally and the objective realm as not being identical to the mind—how then could this be called the contemplation of the Perfect Teaching’s absolute non-relation?

Furthermore, the three bodies of Amitābha are taken as the Dharmakāya, and my own three contemplations are taken as the Prajñā; when the contemplation is perfected and the Buddha is seen, this is itself liberation.
To bring forth one while possessing all three is like the new character *i* (the three dots).
Since the contemplation of the Buddha is thus, the contemplation of all environments and inhabitants (*niśraya-vastu*) follows the same principle; they are not different paths.
If this meaning is not clarified, it does not constitute the present contemplation of the Buddha.
This is explained in two parts:
first, tracing the name from its Sanskrit origin.
"Immeasurable Life" (Wuliangshou) is already a Chinese translation; in the Sanskrit language of India, it is called Amitābha.
II. From "The Origin of the Buddha" (*Buddha-ben*) onwards, the section on "Emerging from the True to Enter the Conventional" has two parts.
First, regarding the original absence of the three [bodies], it marks the Immeasurable Life (*Amitāyus*).

This is that which is immeasurable yet functions as a measure; thus, the title itself already speaks of "lifespan" (*āyus-pramāṇa*). Since this lifespan is established in dependence upon the body, it constitutes three meanings. Therefore, one discusses existence and non-existence by way of these three meanings.
That which is called "Buddha" refers to ultimate awakening.

Since both principle and wisdom have reached their limit, both the beginning and the fundamental are forgotten; being without marks and without name, it cannot be described or demonstrated—how, then, could one establish its person or its lifespan?
2. "In accordance with" and below, [the text] establishes [the categories] in common with worldly convention; this has two parts:
first, listing the three bodies, each with three aspects.
According to the ultimate awakening of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it is impossible to speak of a body or a lifespan.
For the sake of liberating sentient beings, one accords with worldly conventions to establish names and characteristics; thus, the three bodies (trikāya) and the three lifespans are taught.
In this regard, the true Buddha is not threefold, yet appears as such in accordance with the world. However, one must understand the intended meaning behind both existence and non-existence.

To say that the Buddha fundamentally has no body and no lifespan means only that he lacks the three types of existence—those based on marks, those following worldly sentiment, and those based on conceptualization; it does not mean that he lacks the wondrous body and other attributes fully endowed by nature. Therefore, the true Buddha ultimately encompasses all dharmas of both the pure and the defiled.
If there were nothing at all, how would this differ from the ultimate truth expounded by the Hīnayāna?

Therefore, that the ultimate is non-existent while the conventional exists, and that the ultimate exists while the conventional is non-existent, are both *siddhāntas* (established tenets); one must not adhere to either one-sidedly.

The meaning of the present text is that it establishes the three bodies (trikāya) to explain Amitāyus; fearing that one might cling to them as being definitively existent, it first states that the Buddha originally has no three bodies, and they are spoken of as existing only in accordance with worldly convention.
Having attained this understanding, one will encounter no impediment in distinguishing the three bodies, the three lifespans, and the three measures.
Second, from "The Dharma-body" onwards, there is an explanation of the three bodies and their three meanings, which is divided into two parts:
first, the distinction according to their meanings; second, their mutual identity based on principle.
Because the subsequent text exhaustively clarifies the principle of mutual fusion, we shall now provisionally analyze each of the two natures according to their cultivation.
The first [nature] is further divided into three parts;
the first is the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), which has two sections:
First, the individual explanation has three parts.
First, regarding the *dharmakāya*: the Master explains the term "dharma" by setting aside its general sense for a specific one.

Generally, both sentient beings and Buddhas take the *dharmatā* as their guiding principle; however, while the nine realms [of sentient beings] take it as their guide, they act in opposition to it—just as a person may rely upon a teacher yet fail to follow that teacher’s instructions.
Only the Buddhas, from their initial aspiration, practice in accordance with the Dharma, and are now able to fully realize the nature of reality that accords with the Dharma.
Thus, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "That which the Buddhas take as their teacher is the Dharma; for the Dharma is eternal."
Because all Buddhas also constantly accord with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), they take the Dharma as their teacher.
In reality, it is not that the teacher and the essence of the teacher are distinct; therefore, they take the very Dharma that is the teacher as their own body.
Although it is called a "body," it has already transcended the five aggregates (skandhas); therefore, it is neither material substance nor mental consciousness.

Material form is the first aggregate, while mental consciousness constitutes the other four aggregates. Since it is neither an aggregate nor a sense base (āyatana) or element (dhātu), it is not comprised within the three categories of the dharmas that sustain and categorize existence.

This has already excluded both *paricchinna-bheda* (segmented) and *pariṇāma-vikāra* (transformative) [death], demonstrating that it is subsumed within the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth of birth and death.

Furthermore, its material substance distinguishes it from the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body), its mental consciousness distinguishes it from the *vipākaja* (retribution), and the three categories [of the *dharmaskandha*] distinguish it from the causes; since it is none of these, by what name shall it be designated?
For the sake of the capacities of sentient beings, one forcibly designates *dharmatā* as the *dharmakāya*.
Second, regarding "Dharmatā" and below, it concerns longevity (*āyus*).
Longevity, which maintains continuity, directly depends upon the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

The present "life of the dharma-nature" (dharmatā-āyus) is neither the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) obtained as retribution consisting of consciousness, breath, and warmth, nor is it the life that maintains these three factors in conjunction.

To manifest its virtue for the sake of sentient beings, it is pointed out that the dharma-nature does not undergo transformation through the eight phases nor change across the nine periods; it is provisionally designated as "life."
3. From "This lifespan" below, [the text discusses] measure.
Regarding the measure of lifespan, one would normally discuss its length and brevity, as well as its extension and contraction.
However, this lifespan of the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) truly lacks such characteristics of measurable quantity; this [section] thus provides a general clarification.

If one were to distinguish them separately, the long would be the *vipākabuddha* (retribution Buddha) and the short would be sentient beings; that which can extend or contract is the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body).
Since it does not possess such measurements, for the sake of establishing contemplation, one forcibly points out that the lifespan of the Dharma is equal in measure to empty space.
2. From "This is" onwards is the general demonstration.

The three meanings of the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) are not a body as an aggregate of the *skandhas*, nor is it a lifespan obtained through retribution, nor is it a measure of length; they are inconceivable, for one forcibly speaks of a body, a lifespan, and a measure with respect to the *dharmatā*.
II. The Reward Body (Sambhogakāya), in two parts:
A. The existence of the reward body in accordance with the Dharma, in two parts:
1. Citing the sutras.
"Recompense" (*pāo*) refers to a reward in return.
Cultivation is the cause; being moved by a wondrous recompense is the returning of that cause.
Regarding the wisdom-virtue (*jñāna-guṇa*) realized in the *Lotus Sūtra*, the scripture states: "The light of wisdom shines immeasurably; it is obtained through long-cultivated practice."
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* realizes the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
These two fruits of virtue are called "retribution" (*vipāka*) because they respond to the cultivation of causes.
Second, from the phrase "Suchness" (*tathatā*) onwards, the characteristics are explained.
At the time of experiencing retribution, what are its characteristics like?
Therefore, this is clarified by means of one dharma and two metaphors.
For instance, if the name is not different [from the object], yet the observed aspect is distinct, it cannot be called "like the object."
If there were an object external to wisdom, it could not be called "as-it-is" (tathatā) like wisdom.

Regarding the two types of "as-it-is" for each: the "as-it-is" of the object is as-it-is in relation to wisdom, and the "as-it-is" of wisdom is as-it-is in relation to the object; because this is the case for both object and wisdom, they attain profound resonance (yǐngmíng).

Wisdom is termed "pervasive" (tong); therefore, it is distinguished by the fruit-consciousness of bodhi—namely, the wisdom of unsurpassed bodhi that is in resonance with and merged into the realm of dharmatā.

First, the metaphor of the box and its lid is raised to illustrate their correspondence; fearing that one might think that although the edges of the box and lid meet perfectly, two distinct forms ultimately remain, the metaphor of water and milk is further raised to illustrate their mutual merging, so that one may know that the beginning and the source are both identical to the nature of awakening.
When their substance merges indistinguishably, just like water and milk, it is revealed that there is no wisdom outside the object and no object outside wisdom.
Water and milk can be seen [as distinct].
Second, regarding "Dharmakāya" and below, three aspects are established within the *saṃbhogakāya*: namely, body, lifespan, and measure.

Regarding the statement that each of the three [bodies] is the *dharmakāya*: it is because the *saṃbhogakāya* and wisdom are in profound accord, and there is no *saṃbhogakāya* apart from the *dharma*.
First, concerning "body":
the phrase "non-body" means that it is not the case that the *nirmāṇakāya* possesses a body with delimited boundaries.
"Non-non-body" means that it is not the retributive Buddha’s body of limited dimensions.

Furthermore, "not being a body" means it is not existence; "non-non-body" means it is not emptiness. The Dharma-body of the Middle Way is the essence of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*); initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*) merges with this, and even the capacity for such merging is forgotten.
In order to establish the contemplation, it is provisionally termed "retributive wisdom" (*vipākajñāna*).
Second, from the phrase "Dharma-life" (*dharmāyuṣ*) onwards, the life-span is clarified.
As for the statement "not a life-span," it means that it is not a life-span in the conventional sense of being a continuous, sustaining force.
Regarding "not non-life," it means that retributive wisdom does not fail to sustain life.
This double negation of the two extremes reveals the dharma-body within the profound mystery.
The intent behind this provisional designation is the same as in the preceding section.
3. Below "The Measure of Dharma" (*dharmapramāṇa*), the measure is clarified.
It is neither a measure that ought to exist, nor is it a measureless retribution; furthermore, the meaning of its non-duality is identical to that of the lifespan of the body.
III. The Response Body (nirmāṇakāya). This has three parts.
First, clarifying its manifestation in response to sentient beings, which has three sub-sections.
First, the body.
Like an echo responding to a valley, its magnitude follows the sound;
like a mirror manifesting forms, its beauty or ugliness depends on the object.
Responding to the stimuli of the myriad things, it manifests superior or inferior bodies.
2. From "should be the same" downwards, [it concerns] lifespan.
Since the body is already the same as that of other beings, how could lifespan differ according to their capacities?
3. From "should be the same" downwards, [it concerns] size.
According to what is appropriate, whether long or short, he demonstrates both the measurable and the immeasurable.
Second, from "Wisdom bestows" (*jñāna-yacchati*) onwards, it clarifies the response based on the two kinds of existence;
this has three parts: first, the Dharma.
Wisdom is the reward body (saṃbhogakāya) and substance is the dharma body (dharmakāya); these two merge in profound unity, such that their application is boundless.
Second, the section beginning with "like water" provides an analogy.
High-quality gold must be mixed with mercury before it can be applied to objects;
lacking this one condition, the gold has no application for coating.
Third, from "merit" onwards, the synthesis [of the analogy and the teaching].
The merit of the wisdom of retribution accords with the Dharma-body; wherever there are sentient beings with receptive capacities, there is nowhere it does not respond.
Third, from "is able to" onwards, it clarifies that the response pervades the three lands, in two parts:
first, it clarifies both the reward and the response bodies together.
Second, from "having measure" (*sānta*) onwards, the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is shown alone.
Regarding the first meaning: what was explained above as "retribution" (*vipāka*) refers only to the hidden dharma, which is the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*).

Now, it is clarified that the manifested response consists of two traces: by means of the eternally abiding response of the *parasaṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body for others), in contrast to the impermanent response of the *janmakāya* (birth-body), these two modes of activity are demonstrated; therefore, both the bodies and so forth are explained together.
The "body" (kāya) refers to the birth-body (janmakāya), which possesses delimited characteristics; therefore, it is called "body.
The "non-body" refers to the retribution-body (vipākakāya), which lacks delimited characteristics; therefore, it is called "non-body."
The *Shorter Prajñāpāramitā* states: "That which the Buddha calls 'non-body' is named the 'Great Body. This Great Body is the *parabhogakāya* (body of enjoyment for others).
As it is a body without limits, its lifespan is eternal; therefore, it is immeasurable.
The body has its limits, and since life is impermanent, it is finite.
These two applications abide according to the two principles of the True (zhen) and the Middle (zhong), while sentient beings perceive them through the two consciousnesses of karma and activity.
Abiding in principle is explained at length in the *Jinguang Commentary*.
As for the two consciousnesses, the details are found in the *Awakening of Faith*.

To clarify the essential meaning of the treatise: when viewed from the perspective of the *shishi* (phenomenal consciousness), it perceives the boundaries of form; therefore, it is called the "Responsive Buddha" (*yìngfó*).
When perceived by the karmic consciousness, it is free from the marks of spatial limitation; therefore, it is the Reward Body (Sambhogakāya).
This meaning will be analyzed later in the *Foshuanguanchao* (Commentary on the Contemplation of the Buddha).
The practitioner must know that the Constant Body is immeasurable and universally responds within the three lands.
Since impermanence is limited, they should only dwell together.

Why is this? It is because those who perceive the Body of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) through the partial realization of the true retribution capacity are people of the Expedient Land who receive only the Separate and Perfect Teachings.
Although the physical marks of the Buddhas they perceive may appear small or inferior, these are not *janma-kāya* (birth-bodies); they are all *vipāka-buddhas* (retribution-Buddhas).

If those in the Land of Common Residence possess the capacities for the four teachings and receive the *vyākaraṇa* (distinct) or *vaipulya* (perfect) teachings, they are able to behold the retribution-Buddha.

Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clarifies that [the Buddha] eternally dwells on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states that he preaches the Dharma until the end of the future; furthermore, various Mahāyāna scriptures show that within the manifested form (nirmāṇakāya), one perceives this sublime and extraordinary body of the Dharma-nature (dharmatā). Thus, we know that the eternal body universally responds throughout the three lands.

If it were an impermanent body, it would only be able to dwell together [with others] to guide those of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings capacities, thereby generating the wholesome roots of ordinary beings.
The second meaning is divided into two parts:
first, clarifying the two meanings of being finite.
Regarding what has been explained above, the three lands manifested externally beyond the self-enjoyment [body] are all termed "response" (nirmāṇa).

Although other enjoyment bodies are termed "response" in relation to their specific objects (the capacities of sentient beings), they are also termed "retribution" (vipāka) because they are actualized by real causes; they are not merely functional manifestations adapted to the capacities of beings.
If we discuss the body and lifespan that follow objects and conditions, varying in their dimensions and duration, these must be explained in terms of the common, provisional realm.
Therefore, I shall now specifically demonstrate the characteristics of the response-body (nirmāṇakāya), which merely distinguishes two types of finite measures within the realm of the measurable.
These two modes of cognition, because they rely on the *shishi* (active consciousness) and perceive only emptiness, belong exclusively to the impermanent.

If, however, one relies on the *yeshi* (karmic consciousness) and perceives non-emptiness, then this very impermanence is in its entirety permanence; thus, the two functions of permanence and impermanence are mutually identical, like two birds flying together.

If the faculties of those in the two higher lands were to cease and transform, it too would be impermanent; however, because it does not undergo the eight characteristics [of conditioned phenomena], it is provisionally called "permanent.
Regarding the phrase "seven hundred" and so forth, the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra* states: "The Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati asked:
'How long is the Buddha’s lifespan?'"
The Buddha directed him to travel eastward, past thirty-two thousand buddha-fields, to the land of Adorned, where he was to inquire after the Buddha Sovereign King of Illuminating Adornment.
That Buddha replied:
"As is the lifespan of Śākyamuni, so too is mine."
"If you wish to know, my lifespan is seven hundred asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Having heard this, Kaṭabha turned back and informed the Buddha.
Ānanda said:
"That Buddha is merely another name for Śākyamuni.
Although his capacity was superior and his vision more extensive, because seven hundred [aeons] can still be counted, this too is a measure of the finite.
If one considers Amitābha, neither humans nor devas can count him; therefore, he is the "immeasurable within the measurable.
Second, from "The Responsive Buddha" (*nirmāṇakāya*) onwards, it concludes that all responsive buddhas are likewise so.

Since all Buddhas have fully realized the three bodies (*trikāya*), their response-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) manifest to sentient beings; as the lifespans of those beings vary in length, do the Buddhas not accordingly manifest two different measures for each?
Thus, while Amitābha manifests a long lifespan, he is also able to manifest a short one; and while Śākyamuni manifests a short lifespan, he is also able to manifest a long one.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 36, states: "One should know that Śākyamuni Buddha also possesses a pure land, such as the land of Amitābha Buddha."
"Amitābha Buddha also possesses an unadorned and impure land, just like the land of Śākyamuni Buddha.
Furthermore, the thirty-eighth [chapter] states: "Because this Jambudvīpa is evil, the lifespan of Śākyamuni must be short."
"Because other places are excellent, the Buddha's lifespan should be long.

Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 22, states: "Thirty-two sands of Ganges rivers to the west of here lies the land of Anabhibhūta; its adornments are like those of the Land of Peace and Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), and it is there that I appear in the world."
All of these follow the capacities of sentient beings.
Second, from the word "However" (*rán*) onwards, the text establishes their mutual identity based on principle.

In the preceding discussion of the three bodies: the Dharma-body is inherently existent; the Reward-body is accomplished through cultivation; and the Response-body is manifested according to circumstances.
These words may seem to imply laxity; however, one must know that the two modes of cultivation—retribution and practice—are inherently present within the fundamental nature (*xingde*).

Although they are inherent qualities of nature, the aspects of cultivation remain distinct and vivid. Practice arises entirely from nature, and cultivation is entirely contained within nature. Thus, the three (nature, cultivation, and their union) merge into an indistinguishable unity, beyond the reach of thought or description.
Regarding the phrase "it is not so" and so forth: as discussed above in the vertical analysis, this demonstrates that they are not identical.
If it is said that the three bodies and their lifespans are inherently complete [within the Buddha], this demonstrates that they are not distinct.

If one forms an understanding based on the dualities of identity and difference, or unity and multiplicity, one deviates from the essence of the perfectly eternal Dharma that is expressed: because it is three while being one, it is not horizontal; because it is one while being three, it is not vertical; being neither vertical nor horizontal, it is inconceivable.
To interpret it in this manner is to harmonize with the profound and wondrous texts that can express [the truth].
