II. Discerning the Essence (*tattva*). In the preceding text, the explanation of the speaker and the spoken, as well as the contemplator and the contemplated, all pertained to the designating names (*nāman*).
Now, we discern the essence designated by these names, desiring that students, like obtaining the fish through the trap, may seek out the names to reveal the essence.

Seeking the name is intended for the forgetting of names; revealing the essence is to know that there is no separate essence. This is the subtle intent of our Master in explaining the names and defining the essence.
Furthermore, one should understand that the explanation of the names is general, as it encompasses the three dharmas collectively;
the three chapters are specific, as they distinguish the three dharmas individually.
Therefore, in explaining the two names—the general and the specific—none fail to encompass the three aspects of meaning, teaching, practice, and principle.

Since the Buddha who speaks possesses the three bodies (*trikāya*), the contemplative objects he teaches each likewise possess these three; thus it is said that the "Explanation of Names" generally covers these three dharmas. The "Chapter on the Substance" specifically concerns the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); the "Chapter on the Thesis and Function" specifically pertains to the other two; and the "Chapter on the Characteristics of the Teachings" distinguishes between the general and the specific.

Although the substance (*tǐ*) of the present discussion resides in a single dharma, that one must necessarily possess the three; thus, we clarify the three meanings of substance as *lǐ* (ritual/form), *dǐ* (foundation/bottom), and *dá* (penetration/attainment).

Although these three meanings are discussed, they pertain only to the three aspects within the Dharmakāya; the fact that each of the other two [kāyas] also possesses its own three has not yet been clarified. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa xuán* states: "Because it proclaims the secret treasury in its entirety, it accords with its name."

The Dharma-body encompasses all phenomena, neither vertical nor horizontal, as its essence; Prajñā encompasses all phenomena like the three eyes on a face, as its principle; and Liberation encompasses all phenomena like the three dots of the syllable *ī*, as its function.
This exposition is precisely its teaching; it not only establishes the meaning of the sūtra’s essence, but also clarifies other meanings.

The text concludes. Now, I shall set forth its underlying intent: because emptiness and the provisional are both the Middle, the three [truths] belong to the essence (*tattva*); because the provisional and the Middle are both emptiness, the three belong to the thesis (*siddhānta*); and because the Middle and emptiness are both the provisional, the three belong to the function (*vṛtti*).
This liberation is specifically likened to three dots, for a dot is a written character;
the principle corresponds to Prajñā, which is specifically likened to three eyes, for the eye is able to illuminate;
the three aspects of the Dharmakāya are specifically merged, whether vertical or horizontal, to manifest the state beyond thought.

Thus we know that the "Explanation of Names" (Shiming) provides a general overview of the nine dharmas, while the "Discrimination of Substance" (Bianti) specifically addresses the three within the Dharma-body.
Yet the nine are not too many and the three are not too few; this precisely constitutes the meaning of the general and the specific within the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
This section has two parts:
first, restating the premise to provide a brief demonstration.

The name is secondary and thus a guest; the substance is primary and thus the host. The name is a provisional designation; the substance is the actual reality. Under every name, there exists its corresponding reality.
II. Below, in the "Commentary" (*Śāstra*), the primary substance is correctly explained in four parts:
First, determining the essence based on two passages.

All phenomena, in their own place, are neither arising nor ceasing; they are neither existent nor empty; they have no agent and no object; they are free from the characteristics of verbal expression, free from the characteristics of names and words, and free from the characteristics of mental conditions.
To be free from these characteristics is called the true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of signlessness.
Who does not possess it?
What dharma is not thus?
If one speaks of realization through direct knowledge, it belongs solely to the Buddhas.
Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "Only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully exhaustively comprehend the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena."

Regarding those who profess the doctrine of inherent perfection: from the very first moment, they employ the Buddha-wisdom to illumine objects; thus, they are able to believe in and understand the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.

Having understood the true mark, they also understand the true nature, true substance, true power, true function, true cause, true condition, true fruit, true retribution, and the true equality of beginning and end of all phenomena.

Since these ten dharmas are real, they constitute the truly born and truly awakened Buddha, the true reliance and the true correctness; not a single form or scent is anything other than the Middle Way, and all phenomena are the Buddha-dharma.
Since all things are real and there is nothing beyond reality, how can it be said that "all else is the work of Māra"?
One should understand that this statement uses principle to distinguish from emotional attachment.

If one defines the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) as being free from mental conditions and the characteristics of subject and object, then the slightest appearance of such marks constitutes the work of Māra. Therefore, from the Separate Teaching (pratyekabuddha-yāna) downward, including the dharmas of the six realms of existence, all possess the characteristics of mental conditions involving subject and object; Māra is able to describe these, and they are all termed the work of Māra.
Therefore, know that all things are both demons and Buddhas; when distinguished by emotional attachment, all are deviant, but when free from emotional discrimination, all are correct.

Now, by simplifying emotional attachments and grasping the principle as the essence of the sūtra, one should know that the entire reality (dharmatā) is luminously manifest; this is termed the True Mind and also called Original Enlightenment. Because the substance of enlightenment is all-pervasive, all phenomena are ultimately real.

If one points to its essential core, it does not depart from the present thought of discrimination; this thought is itself original enlightenment (mūla-bodhi), and this enlightenment is the very substance of the sutra—there is no separate substance of the sutra that serves as its expressed meaning.

By means of this awakened mind observing the primary and secondary realms, subject and object are immediately severed and all dualistic dependencies are forgotten; thus, the essence of wondrous contemplation is established from this point onward.
Were it otherwise, why would it be necessary to first attain the substance before establishing the core tenets of the Sūtra?
Regarding the Seal of the True Aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇamudrā*): a "seal" (*mudrā*) refers to a seal of authentication, as well as a sign of faith, and a definition of certainty.

It is by means of this that one determines the scope of the Great and Small Vehicles, as well as what is heterodox or orthodox; only when the principle accords with the Buddha’s intent may it be trusted and followed.
The three seals of the Hīnayāna consist of the two seals of impermanence and non-self, which seal *saṃsāra*, and the single seal of cessation (*śānti*), which seals *nirvāṇa*.
Because *nirvāṇa* in the Hīnayāna is distinct from *saṃsāra*, each is sealed separately.
If what is expounded accords with this, then one can trust and accept that these are Sūtras of the Hīnayāna and not the teachings of Māras or non-Buddhists.

The single seal of the Mahāyāna is precisely the single true reality (*bhūtatathatā*); the two kinds of birth-and-death and the threefold virtue of *nirvāṇa* are identical in essence, being ultimately real.
The meaning accords with this; one may thus believe and accept that this is a Mahāyāna sūtra, neither Hīnayāna nor non-Buddhist.
Now, based on this sūtra, the perfect and real is "Great.
If one follows those treatises where the Tripiṭaka is contrasted with the Vaipulya, both the general and specific teachings are also termed the "Single Seal."

Now, not grasping at duality, but taking only the perfect true mark as the "Single Seal," then the person who speaks, the objects of contemplation—the environment and its inhabitants—and the four kinds of purity and impurity, as well as the five heinous crimes, are all non-dual in their nature.
By means of this single seal, it constitutes the authentic body of the sūtra.
Second, from "Immeasurable" onwards, it serves as the point of convergence for the four chapters.
Regarding "Immeasurable Merit" and so forth, these represent the application of the sūtra’s purpose.
The power and function of the Sūtra are also termed "merit" (*guṇa*); its power possesses the efficacy of extinguishing evil, while its function possesses the virtue of generating goodness.
Because it extinguishes all evils and generates all goodness, this merit receives immeasurable names.
These merits collectively adorn the essential body, much like a sovereign who governs disorder and nurtures the people.
Adorning the holy person with these merits constitutes the various practices that form the core of the sutra.
Arising from principle, practice fully embodies that principle; it is like water forming waves, yet the waves ultimately return to the water.
Since the school's tenets must accord with the fundamental essence, it is said: "Having already proceeded toward."
In general, it encompasses the myriad practices; specifically, it refers to the sixteen contemplations; thus, it is called "Various Practices" (*saṃghāṭa*).
"Discourse and Question-and-Answer" is the title of the sutra; the name that expresses [the meaning] resides in the discourse.

The meaning of the words is profound and abstruse; furthermore, it requires various questions and answers for exposition and analysis in order to establish the title of the sutra and manifest its true essence.
Question:
A title serves as a name; how could it ever involve such things as questions and answers?
Answer:
"Name" (nāma) refers to that which can express the essence [of a teaching]; every sentence in a single section is capable of expressing such names.

For example, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the ten kinds of wondrousness regarding the original and the trace constitute its name; however, because the title serves as the general designation, the name is explained by means of the title.
The remaining four meanings all pervade from beginning to end; therefore, they constitute the title of this single sutra.
Phrases such as "questioning, answering, elucidating, and debating" proceed from the latter back to the former, demonstrating the dharmas to which one returns.
It is not that "teaching" (jiao) is distinct from "name" (ming); rather, it is subsumed within the term itself.

To receive [the Dharma] for oneself is called "name," while transforming others is called "teaching. Although self and other differ, both are capable of signifying; thus, one knows that the four chapters ultimately converge into a single essence.
III. From "The Parable of the Multitude" below, his supremacy is revealed through two metaphors.
Within the four chapters, he is like the North Star, around which all the stars revolve;
he is also like the Eastern Sea, to which all waters flow as their source.
Because these four chapters never depart from the essence for even a moment, there is no principle among all dharmas that is not established.
Since the essence of the sutra is thus, how could one not discern it?
Fourth, the section beginning with "Therefore, by... concludes and demonstrates this through a single seal.
Third, following the section on "the Calligrapher," the essential nature (*tǐ*) and its virtues (*dé*) are fully elucidated.
While the "nature" corresponds to the "explanation of the name" (*shìmíng*), it pertains solely to one virtue, namely the *dharmakāya*.

This is because, within the explanation of the name, the three dharmas were presented collectively; although those of sharp faculties may understand this, those of dull faculties have not yet clarified it.

Why is this? Because the general introductory text carries the function of the thesis, its essence is intermingled therein, and emotional conceptualizations cannot be easily forgotten; thus, the original nature is difficult to manifest.
Therefore, following the general introduction, the spiritual source is shown specifically, eternally distinct from the four māras, as all phenomena are ultimately real.
Regarding that single dot above the circle and the character *ī*: it transcends thought and deliberation, and is neither function nor doctrine. Yet its nature is harmonious;

"one" is not fixed as one, just as the dot of the character *ī* does not exist in isolation. Therefore, the direct Dharma-body is not merely the Dharma-body; the Dharma-body must necessarily possess Prajñā and Vimukti. Thus, the essence is separately revealed to discuss these three meanings.

Although the three virtues are manifested, the intent lies in the Dharma-body; because emptiness and the provisional are both the Middle, these three names are clarified as the virtues of its essence.
Regarding the three aspects of the Middle:
first, the Dharma-body is elucidated through the meaning of ritual propriety (*li*).
Since the *Shu* has already explained the *ti* (essence/body) by means of the *li* (ritual), I shall now explain the *ti* by means of the *li*.
Ritual distinguishes between the honorable and the humble, its intent being to exalt the sovereign and the father.

While the preceding clarification of demonic matters has already eliminated partiality and heterodoxy, what I shall now examine regarding ministers and sons concerns the fundamental application: thus, the essence of the sovereign and the father is itself the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
The myriad dharmas that serve as the teachers of all Buddhas converge here; its essence is neither cultivated nor realized, and its principle transcends words and thought.
Desiring to direct the mind toward it, one forcibly designates it as the "Ultimate Noble.
This is Original Enlightenment, which is neither quiescence nor illumination.
This is also the dharma-nature, which is neither deep nor vast.
The ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is called the virtue of the original nature dharmakāya.

Seeking the expressive names in order to recognize this essence, because the essence is manifest through practice, it enables those who cultivate contemplation to take this essential virtue as the essence of that basis and its manifestations; each being most noble and supreme, they constitute the wondrous thesis.
Second, from "Furthermore" onwards, prajñā is elucidated in terms of its "bottom" (tī).

Since the emptiness of qualities (*guṇa-śūnyatā*) is itself the Middle Way, the quality of prajñā is the bottom of all phenomena; it is also termed the "source," the "deep reservoir," and the "limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*).
If one attains the central essence (*madhyama-bhāva*), one is then able to exhaustively fathom and manifest it.
The *Śāstra* speaks of "Prajñāpāramitā," which is precisely the Prajñā of Real Mark (*lakṣaṇa-prajñā*).
The Buddha, through the Prajñā of Contemplative Observation (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*), realizes this essence of wisdom within all phenomena; therefore, it is said to be "fathoming the bottom."

However, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is profoundly deep and without bottom or limit; as for what is called "reaching the bottom," it is truly because the Buddha, through wisdom that is itself without bottom or limit, realizes it in accordance with its true nature—this is what is meant by the term "reaching the bottom."
Those of the seven stages of expedient means, because they possess a wisdom with a bottom, cannot reach the source and depth of all dharmas.
As for those of the Perfect Teaching, from the stage of "immediate identity with names," they exhaust the depths of the Perfection of Wisdom through the mind of faith and understanding;
at the five grades of contemplative practice, they exhaust the depths.
The ten stages of faith reach the bottom through resemblance;
the forty-one stages reach the bottom through partial realization;
only Buddha-to-Buddha reaches the ultimate bottom.

When the essence of the sūtra is analyzed through this fundamental meaning, it reveals the profound Dharma-nature and the ultimate emptiness of the primary truth, which is termed the virtue of *prajñā*.

By investigating the name to recognize the essence, and because that essence is manifest, one practices; thus, the practitioner, by means of this essential virtue, exhaustively explores each aspect of both the environment and its inhabitants to their very depths, thereby perfecting the wondrous thesis.
Third, from "Furthermore" onwards, the virtue of liberation is elucidated in terms of the realization of meaning.
Because the provisional is identical to the Middle Way, the virtue of liberation is the essence of sovereign mastery over all phenomena, and it further possesses all true names and meanings.

If one realizes this essence, one will attain mastery and thorough penetration regarding all phenomena; furthermore, concerning all the diverse names of the mundane and supramundane, one will understand the many within the one and the one within the many.
The treatise says "Prajñā," which refers here to the Prajñā of the True Mark (lakṣaṇa-prajñā).
Since Prajñā and Liberation (vimukti) differ in name but are identical in meaning, they are mentioned interchangeably.
The preceding section clarified the fundamental principle: by means of the Prajñā of Contemplative Observation (pratyavekṣaṇā-prajñā), one exhaustively penetrates the foundation of the True Mark.
Now, to clarify the meaning: through the *prajñā* of words and letters (*nāma-prajñā*), the various names of the *prajñā* of ultimate reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa-prajñā*) are explained.
Because those at the seven stages of skillful means are deluded regarding this essence, they become obstructed and hindered by these various different names.
In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), there is realization through names, realization through contemplative practice, realization through semblance, and realization through partial truth.

Here, the Buddha’s ultimate realization is cited; when the meaning of "realization" is used to define the essence, it reveals the significance of the Dharma-nature as the immeasurable Tathāgatagarbha, which is termed the virtue of true-nature liberation.

By means of these essential qualities, the practitioner of contemplation penetrates each and every aspect of both the environment and its inhabitants without obstruction, thereby perfecting the sublime thesis.
Third, the clarification of the thesis (*zong*).
"Thesis" refers to the essential core.
The essential point of this sutra lies in cultivating the wondrous contemplation of the mind to attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
This mental contemplation is precisely the three contemplations within a single mind; its characteristics have already been explained in detail within the section on defining the names.
The characteristics of the perceived land have been fully discussed in this text.
Now, regarding the wondrous essence of this sutra, it lies in these causes and effects.
For now, let us divide them into two parts:
First, the heading and enumeration.
Second, the detailed explanation from "There is a person" onwards, which has two parts:
first, the selection and indication of the essence of the school.
Because many people are confused regarding the characteristics of identity and difference within the essence of this school, it is necessary to clarify and demonstrate them.
The text has two parts; first, the clarification, which is divided into two: [The text continues with the specific clarifications.]
First, distinguishing that the essence of the school is one, in two parts:
first, restating the words to briefly refute [the opponent].
The "school" (zong) refers to cause and effect, which belongs to the realm of phenomena (dharma).
That their essence is of a single nature belongs to the realm of principle (*li*).
Although they are not mutually abandoned, the two meanings must be distinguished.
To insist dogmatically that they are one is truly contrary to the meaning; therefore, it is said, "it is not used."
II. From "What is it? below, there is an extensive refutation based on the meaning, which has three parts.
First, the refutation according to the meaning.
"Thesis" (zong) refers to the intended goal; this goal consists of both the fruit and the principle.
Attaining the fruit necessarily depends on the cause;
if one is to attain the principle, it is essential to cultivate contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

Since there are degrees of clarity and obscurity in contemplation, and there is realization or non-realization of the principle, both constitute cause and effect; therefore, it is said that "the tenets are twofold."
The essence is fundamentally principle; although contemplation tends toward that principle, the principle itself is neither bright nor obscure.
Cause and effect depend upon principle, yet the principle is not cause and effect.
It is like waves depending on water: while the waves have a thousand variations, the water is always one.
Therefore, it is said that "the essence is non-dual.
If one does not speak of all phenomena as being of the same rational nature, it cannot be called the essence of a Mahāyāna sūtra; hence it is said that "duality is not the essence."
Whether it concerns the two dharmas of cultivation and realization, or cause and effect, neither constitutes the essential tenet (zongqiu) established by the Buddhist scriptures.
Second, the section beginning with "Like a beam" establishes a metaphor to refute [the opponent's position].
Although the empty house and its beams and pillars are not separate from one another, if one were to claim they are identical, then there would be no distinction between the void and the substantial.
Third, following "The Essential Body" (zōngtǐ), the faults are raised and the conclusion is reached.
2. Distinguishing the Differences in the Essential Body (*svabhāva*): Part Two.
First, restating the statement to refute [the opponent].
Although the refutation is one, one must not cling to differences.
If they were definitively distinct, then the two things would exist in isolation.

If the thesis were different from the essence, it would not arise from the complete nature as a cultivated attainment; such contemplative practice involving effort would belong to the eight inversions.
Since this does not accord with principle, it cannot be the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong); hence it is said that "it is perverse and inverted, lacking the Seal.
If the essence were of a different school, then principle would not be identical to phenomena; a principle existing apart from phenomena would lack universal pervasiveness in its essence.
If the essence of the dharma-nature were distinct from cause and effect, then all dharmas would consequently exist as separate entities.
Second, from "The Essence of the Thesis" (*zongti*) onwards, the faults [of this position] are raised and concluded.
Second, from "Now it says" onwards, [the text] demonstrates.
Based now on the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sukhāvatī-vyūha-sūtra*, we verify that its fundamental essence is neither fixed as identical nor different.
Thus, that sūtra states: "The cause of the Mahāyāna is the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) of all phenomena."
"The fruit of the Mahāyāna is the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
This true mark is neither different from nor identical to cause and effect; it is not a seal of inverted existence—this is its wondrous aspect (*miao-zong*).
Cause and effect and the true mark are neither one nor many; it is not a principle external to phenomena—this is its wondrous essence (*miao-ti*).
How can this be the same as others establishing fixed identity or difference?
Since they have not heard this, how can they speak one-sidedly?
By expounding upon this commentary, one should come to know the essential substance of the school.

To perceive only the objects of conceptualization while failing to apply the three contemplations is precisely the same as the heterodox perversions of the second school, which lack the seal [of truth]; this is truly most lamentable.
Second, from "Now, this" onwards, the essence is clarified through its fundamental principle in three parts:
first, a direct demonstration based on the sutras.

The essential point of the Mahāyāna Dharma lies in the mind; the attributes of the mind are easy to know, whereas the attributes of form are difficult to understand. Thus, the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states: "Because the cause is pervasive, it is easily recognized; because the fruit is remote, it is difficult to know. Therefore, whether observing oneself or others, one practices the contemplation of the mind.

Now, in observing the Pure Land, one must seek it within the mind; for the mind is capable of possessing it and the mind is capable of creating it. "When the mind is defiled, the land is defiled; when the mind is pure, the land is pure. This is still a general indication and has not yet reached the definitive discussion.

To suddenly cultivate the three contemplations within a single mind, wherein this contemplation contemplates the ultimate purity of the environment and inhabitants of the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), is called "purity of mental contemplation.
This contemplation can purify the four Buddha-lands; it is precisely in this way that the essential purport of this sutra is established.
Second, from "The four kinds" downward, there is an extensive explanation based on the lands, in three parts:
first, listing the four lands;
second, from "Each has" downward, establishing the pure and the defiled.
If one explains the meaning according to the literal text, both the teaching and the contemplation will sink into obscurity;
if one employs the meaning to interpret the text, understanding and practice can be brought forth.

In the preceding explanation of the character "contemplation" (*guan*), the text clearly reveals the three contemplations within a single mind (*ekacitta-trivipaśyanā*); furthermore, the text repeatedly indicates that the mind and contemplation constitute the core principle (*mūla*). This culminates in the summary of the core principle, which states: "The wondrous contemplation of cultivating the mind (*cittabhāvanā-maṇyavipaśyanā*) is able to evoke the Pure Land."
Now, regarding the purity and impurity of these four lands as explained in this text, one must rely on this contemplation to establish the causes for the four purities.

If one were to follow various other texts by treating each of the four lands individually and discussing their respective causes, how could one provide a comprehensive synthesis of the preceding and following passages? Furthermore, how could this enable those who hear it to realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?
Regarding the first point, "The five turbidities being light constitutes the purity of the Shared Residence," this purity is very general; one must understand its specific meaning.

For instance, those with the wholesome roots of precepts within the ordinary stages of the Four Teachings are all able to cause the five turbidities to become light and thin, thereby eliciting the purity of the Shared Residence.

Through the complete contemplation of the light and turbid [world], one is moved to perceive the purity of the Land of Common Residence (Sahā), wherein both the environment and its inhabitants are most pure.

As this sutra describes the specific characteristics of each stage from the contemplation of the earth onwards, they differ vastly in nature when compared to the cultivation of various virtuous deeds in other sutras that results in rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī).

Regarding the phrase "the characteristics of essence, analysis, skill, and deficiency, as well as purity and defilement": in this land, the pure characteristics perceived by the multitude are also broad. While the perception of defilement through analytical contemplation (*vikalpa-vidarśanā*) may be found within the Tripiṭaka, the perception of purity through essential contemplation (*tattva-vidarśanā*) does not belong exclusively to those of the Shared Vehicle. In the three teachings of the Mahāyāna, when contrasted with the analytical [teachings] of the Tripiṭaka, all clarify the essential nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*): the Shared Vehicle takes emptiness as its essence; the Distinct Vehicle takes the sequential [stages] as its essence; and the Perfect Vehicle takes the non-sequential as its essence. When these three types of people are born in that [Pure Land], they all perceive pure characteristics.

The person of the Perfect Teaching is most pure, as explained in the *Avalokiteśvara Commentary*. They practice specifically toward the Perfect Teaching; from the seventh stage of faith onward, they perceive that the environment and inhabitants [of their realm] are identical to the Real Reward Land, whereas the stages of abiding, practice, and penetration, as well as the characteristics of their vision, are all inferior.

Now, the wondrous essence of this sutra must differ from that of the three [previous] persons; therefore, it abides together with the "surplus" (yǒuyú) and clarifies the pure marks. Although the phrasing is general, the meaning is specific; one must rely on the passages concerning the sudden contemplation of the preceding and following sections, as well as the words of the *Miaozong*, to interpret this general text so that it returns to its definitive purpose.

Regarding the statement, "Successively or suddenly entering the true retribution of purity or impurity": if we discuss actual realization, this land is inhabited solely by those of the Perfect [Teaching] Saintly stage.

Since the realization of the Separate Teaching’s first bhūmi is identical to that of the Perfect, and they both experience retribution in accordance with reality, how could there be any distinction of superiority or inferiority?

Now, because the ten stages of the path of teaching are not yet fused, the lands manifested by those who attain them differ from those of the person of the Perfect [Teaching]; thus, purity and impurity are distinguished according to the gradual and the sudden.

Regarding the statement "the distinction between the ultimate *sijiguang* (tranquil light) and its purity or impurity": if one considers the Separate Teaching practitioner who attains realization equally with the Perfect, then in discussing *sijiguang*, purity and impurity are distinguished solely by contrasting the true cause against the ultimate fruit of the Perfect.
Now, this treatise discusses the path of teaching as it pertains to the ultimate fruit: by severing only twelve grades of ignorance, the Land of Quiescent Light remains defiled;
only through perfect knowledge that severs forty-two grades is it called ultimately pure.
One must still understand that a person of perfect capacity (yuan-ren) is able to take the principle of the supreme, eternally quiescent light as the substance of contemplation from beginning to end.
What is discussed here in terms of the ultimate refers to the subtle contemplation cultivated by the practitioner who has achieved the "intentionally formed" body (yi-cheng).
Third, below the character "sa," the names and characteristics are explained.
This section merely explains the names of the lands, briefly indicating their purity or impurity.
If one were to discuss specifically the causes capable of inducing the four types of pure lands, they consist solely of the perfect contemplation, as already described above.
Section Four:
First, the explanation of "co-residence" (*sahā-vāsa*).
"Co-residence" refers to persons, while "purity and defilement" refer to lands; that is to say, ordinary beings and sages co-reside in a defiled land.

In the Pure Land, there is likewise the cohabitation of ordinary beings and sages; in both realms, the ordinary beings are real, while the sages encompass both the provisional and the real—their initial realization is the real, and their coming as responsive manifestations is the provisional.
Regarding the phrase "next to nirvāṇa": *nirvāṇa* and *niepan* are simply the new and old transliterations of the same Sanskrit term.
Those born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing have their afflictions subdued and are thus close to nirvāṇa; for this reason, they are said to be "next" [to it].
"All belong to the group of those fixed in rightness" refers to the classification of the three groups (*tri-niyata-rāśi*).
If one were to judge according to the ordinary people of this land who have not yet awakened their resolve, they would belong to the group of those fixed in error (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*);
those who have awakened their resolve and practice without falling back would belong to the group of those not yet fixed (*aniyata-rāśi*).
Those who attain non-retrogression belong to the group of those destined for certainty (samyaktvaniyāma-rāśi).

If one is born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), regardless of whether their status is high or low—even a person who has committed the five heinous crimes (pañcānantarya) and attains rebirth through ten recitations at the moment of death—also attains non-retrogression; therefore, it is said that all are within the group destined for certainty.
The *Awakening of Faith* clarifies that those who first resolve to attain birth there abide in right concentration;
thus, the *Smaller Amitābha Sūtra* states: "All who are born there attain the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*)."
Among the pure lands, the Land of Ultimate Bliss corresponds to the highest grade.

If one practices according to the sixteen contemplation gates (*ṣoḍaśa-vipaśyanā-mukha*) of this present sutra with perfect subtlety, even if pervasive delusions (*paryavasthāna-kleśa*) still persist, one will be born in that land and constantly behold sublime signs, just as the practitioners at the various Mahayana assemblies of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* in this land perceive them.
2. Explanation of "with remainder" (sa-śeṣa), in three parts:
First, explaining the name by way of abandonment through cultivation.
Nine types of practitioners together give birth in that land:
The two [levels] of the Distinct [Teaching], the three [levels] of the Shared [Teaching],
and the two [levels] of practice and abiding in the Distinct [Teaching] all constitute the path of skillful means (*upāyamārga*) once they have cultivated emptiness and the provisional.

Although what is practiced by those with faith in the Perfect [Teaching] is real, it still resides within the semblance-path (*sādṛśamārga*) and is therefore categorized as belonging to the path of skillful means.
The non-arising of the *pratisaṃdhika* [rebirth] occurs when the four *āśrayas* (abodes) are eliminated; with respect to this cultivation and abandonment, it is termed "expedient means" (*upāya*).
Because this abandonment applies both to the general and the specific, it is said to be "with remainder."
2. "Explanation of the Treatise" (Shèlùn) below: This section explains the characteristics based on the sūtras and śāstras.

Although the Hīnayāna claims that all equally enter the *dharmatā*, it maintains that the essence of *dharmatā* is like empty space; thus, if the seeds and fruits are forgotten, there will forever be no bodies or lands.
The essence of the Dharma-nature of the Mahāyāna inherently possesses both form and mind; if one forgets the distinction between cause and fruit, then body and land become vast and expansive.
The *Śāstra* uses "great" to refute the Hīnayāna view that there is no land outside the realm of conditioned existence (*dhātu*), specifically stating: "Beyond the realm, there is a Pure Land."
In the Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) possesses neither form nor mind; therefore, it is specifically said that one "receives the dharmatā-body.
Furthermore, the reference to "encountering other Buddhas" in the *Lotus Sūtra* refers to the Buddhas of the lands with remainder (sopadhiśeṣa).

This refers to those who, after [the Buddha's] parinirvāṇa, do not encounter the four reliances and fail to give rise to true faith; they mistakenly believe that [their own cessation] is ultimate and thus conceive of a "remainder," yet upon receiving the Buddha’s revelation of the provisional, they are able to achieve definitive understanding.
3. From "Among these" onwards, the sharpness or dullness and purity or impurity [of faculties] are clarified.
Regarding those lands, sharpness and dullness are explained solely in reference to the Mahāyāna.
If one has already practiced Madhyamaka in this land and is born there, one is of sharp faculty; the Buddha then teaches the non-sequential dharma for such a person.
If one has not yet practiced Madhyamaka in this land and is born there [in that realm], one will be dull-witted; therefore, the Buddha taught the gradual Dharma for such cases.
Those of sharp faculties dwell above, which is why it is said, "pointing to those above."
"Under the fingers" serves as an illustration of this.
What is seen by those of sharp faculties is identical to that true retribution, and is therefore termed "pure.
What is seen by those of dull faculties has characteristics inferior to the former, and is therefore termed "defiled."

By verifying the former nature through the present sharpness or dullness of faculties, it is evident that only the Perfect [Vehicle] is the true nature, while the preceding three are all analytical. The Separate [Vehicle] is somewhat similar to the Perfect nature within the context of contemplation.
Third, the explanation of the Real Reward [Land] has three parts:
first, explaining the name by way of cause and effect.

Regarding "practicing the path of reality": the person of perfect capacity (yuanren) begins from the first stage, while the person of distinct capacity (bieren) is able to contemplate all phenomena in accordance with reality during the ten stages of dedication.
Now that the Middle Way is opened, one immediately receives a wondrous retribution.

Form and mind are non-dual, and a single hair can contain all lands; this is exclusively the dwelling place of Dharma-body Bodhisattvas. Since even those who approximate the ultimate perfection are thus sublime, how much more so the seven stages of expedient means?
The term "exclusive" (jian) implies a broad inclusion; one should distinguish this well.
2. Below, regarding the *Renwang jing*, the characteristics are explained based on the sutras and treatises.

The *Renwang jing* borrows from the specific [stages] to name the perfect positions (*yuanwei*); the "three worthies" (*sanxian*) and "ten sages" (*shisheng*) are names borrowed from the specific, while those who abide in the fruition of retribution are termed the perfect positions.
Since the three types of worthies dwell together with the ten sages in the same fruit-retribution, this is verified as the true retribution.
If one does not realize the Middle Way, how could one dwell in the true retribution?
Therefore, we know that while the names differ, their meaning belongs to the Perfect [Teaching].
Now, by taking up the fruit and retribution, one realizes the Land of Real Retribution.
Question:
Previously, it was clarified that there are no followers of the Two Vehicles in the Land of Real Retribution; why, then, is it suddenly said here that Kāśyapa rose to dance?
Answer:

One must understand that the four lands have both horizontal and vertical dimensions; furthermore, one must know that these horizontal and vertical aspects exist within a single location. For example, when one proceeds toward a single location in the Shared Land (sahā-lokadhātu), that very place is the Land of True Reward (vipākabhūmi).

If one who has shattered ignorance enters by transforming their body, this is the Dharma-body sharing the same essence and function as the Buddha’s, which is called the wondrous retribution that accords with reality.
Even those with purified six sense-faculties cannot participate in this; how much less could those of the Two Vehicles?
This, then, is a vertical discourse on the true reward (*sambhoga-kāya*) in a single location.

If one has not yet shattered ignorance and remains within the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), it is for the sake of such individuals that the Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas, acting as those capable of being seen, bestow upon them the vision of the land of true reward.

Generally, there are those with the necessary karmic conditions who, although they have not yet destroyed their delusions, have already practiced Madhyamaka; these include those of various capacities at the Avataṃsaka assemblies and other such gatherings, who perceive the inconceivable nature of the Buddha’s body and land through spiritual resonance.

Now, citing the treatise, it is for the purpose of censure within the Vaipulya sutras that the sublime and wondrous five sensory objects of the *sambhogakāya* realm are displayed, causing Kāśyapa and others to suddenly forget their meager desires and give rise to dancing and play.
This is intended to cause the śrāvakas to know the wondrousness of the Great Dharma, so that they may give rise to a heart of admiration and come to despise the Lesser Vehicle.
All such [statements] are merely horizontal discussions from a single perspective regarding the characteristics of the land of true recompense.
Therefore, the eight classes of beings and those of the two vehicles, whose faculties have matured, all behold it.

Now, the inferior is used as a metaphor to reveal the superior land; just as when a being from the human realm dies and falls into the realm of hungry ghosts, they immediately become one of that class and no longer share the common status of a human.
There are those who can perceive that realm within their very own bodies, yet this does not prevent others from likewise seeing its characteristics.
"Falling" is used as a metaphor for entering the True Reward Land vertically; "seeing" is used as a metaphor for discussing the True Reward Land horizontally.
Since this is the case for the Land of Real Reward, it is likewise when discussing the horizontal coexistence of the Lands of Expedient Means and the Land of Peaceful Light.

Within the Land of Co-residence, one discusses the horizontal and vertical dimensions of the three lands; within the Land of Expedient Means, one discusses the horizontal and vertical dimensions of two lands; within the Land of Real Reward, one discusses the horizontal and vertical dimensions of one land. Upon reaching the Land of Peaceful Light, there is neither horizontal nor vertical, nor even the location itself.
Question:

The treatise states that "Kāśyapa was so intensely attached to the superior and exquisite five desires of a bodhisattva that he could not remain still and began to dance. Yet, in the *Lotus Sūtra*, when Kāśyapa recounts how he previously heard of the bodhisattva’s Dharma and his playful mastery of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), he did not give rise to even a single thought of longing or delight. How can these two accounts be reconciled?
Both matters are the dharmas of a bodhisattva; for what reason do love and hatred suddenly become so diametrically opposed?
Answer:
One should know that both states of mind are distinct afflictions (*paryavasthāna*).

To love exquisite desires is to think of them as being of the same substance as oneself; to loathe the saving of sentient beings is like the "dust-sands" beyond the realms. It is like an unworthy son who loves only wealth and status while neglecting his studies.
For example, in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, Śāriputra is rebuked: "As long as the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are not yet exhausted, flowers will adhere to the body.
Because of the fear of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) find their opportunity.
Since they fear birth and death, they take the "dust-sands" (samsāra) to be their fetters and habitual tendencies.

Furthermore, the reference to the "immeasurable clouds of fragrance" from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* refers to the characteristics of the *sahabhū-bhūmi* (the realm of shared existence) and the *vipāka-bhūmi* (the realm of retributive reward), which were previously explained as being manifested horizontally.
3. Below the section "Among these," the gradual and sudden, as well as the pure and impure, are clarified.
4. The explanation of *Jigō* (Sukhāvatī) has three parts:
first, establishing the name by defining its essential nature.
The first three [realms] pertain to phenomena; therefore, their names for the lands are established based on the causes and effects of cultivation and abandonment as practiced by the inhabitants.
This land pertains to principle; therefore, it is named after the three virtues of its fundamental essence.
Question:
Since the three obstacles have not yet been exhausted in the partial realization of the *śānta-prabhāsvara* (tranquil light), how can one establish the name based solely on principle?
Answer:
The limit where hindrances are not yet exhausted belongs to the *sambhogakāya* (recompense body).
Now, regarding the point where cause and effect are partially forgotten, it is called the Middle and Lower Constant Quiescent Light Lands (*nitya-prabhāsvara-kṣetra*).
Second, from "All Buddhas" onwards, the characteristics are shown in terms of those who dwell therein.

The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata dwells within the immeasurable and profoundly deep dharmatā, the sphere of action of all Buddhas, which transcends the pure conduct of all bodhisattvas."
The immeasurable is quiescence; the profound is radiance; the nature of phenomena is permanence.
Furthermore, the *Samantabhadra-darśana-sūtra* states: "Śākyamuni is named Vairocana; the dwelling place of this Buddha is called the Light of Eternal Quiescence."

The sphere accomplished by being encompassed by the perfection of constancy (*nitya-pāramitā*), the sphere established by the perfection of self (*ātma-pāramitā*), the sphere free from the characteristics of body and mind through the perfection of bliss (*sukha-pāramitā*), and the sphere where the characteristics of existence are extinguished through the perfection of purity (*śubha-pāramitā*).

Therefore, we know that this land is established from the ultimate state of the four virtues (*catur-guṇa*). By means of the four *pāramitās*, the three virtues are manifested: permanence (*nitya*) and self (*ātman*) are the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); bliss (*sukha*) is liberation (*vimukti*); and purity (*śubha*) is wisdom (*prajñā*).
The three virtues (trisvabhāva) are mutually inclusive; as each one is discussed in terms of the three, the Dharma-body and the others each possess four virtues.

Although it is said that there are "three times four," in reality they do not constitute twelve; students who understand this will know that this alone is called the secret treasury (guhyagarbha) that is neither vertical nor horizontal.
3. Below "Attaining a Portion" (*fen-de*), it clarifies the distinction between partial and complete, and the pure and the defiled.
"Attaining a portion" is termed "defiled" from the perspective of the one who realizes it;
the name "Eternally Quiescent Light" (*chang-ji-guang*) is established based on the ultimate principle.
III. From "Therefore, by means of" onwards, the meaning is summarized and demonstrated.
Regarding the character *guan* (contemplation) in the title, it clarifies the three perfect contemplations; up to this point, the central tenet has been elucidated.

Initially, it was stated that "by means of the purity of the mind, the Buddha-land is pure," which constitutes the primary purport of the sutra; subsequently, the purity and impurity of the four lands were explained in detail.
Now, the conclusion states: "Therefore, the core tenet of this sutra is that the wondrous contemplation of cultivating the mind can evoke the Pure Land.
If one were not to employ the perfect and wondrous threefold contemplation to evoke the four types of pure lands, then both the opening statement and the concluding text would be entirely useless.
Regarding the third section, the explanation of the title: for what kind of person is the Threefold Contemplation intended?
For what purpose and in what place is it employed?

If one were to claim that the Perfect Threefold Contemplation is required only to evoke the two pure lands of True Reward and Quiescent Light; that if there is a Land of Residual Defilement, one merely cultivates the contemplation of essence-emptiness; and that in the Land of Common Residence, one employs only phenomenal practices without needing the Threefold Contemplation—this interpretation is incorrect.

While the practice of various phenomena based on the essence of emptiness and the two types of pure lands are both causes for rebirth in those lands, they do not represent the primary tenet revealed by this sutra.

This is because this sutra was originally intended for Vaidehī, who, weary of the defilement of the *sahā* world, sought the purity of that same realm; it therefore expounds wondrous contemplation to observe the environment and its inhabitants (*shèngyǐng*). How, then, could one hastily claim that perceiving the purity of the *sahā* world does not require the threefold contemplation?
If the three contemplations are perfected, coarse defilements will fall away first; yet, where could any remaining purity arise?
Could it be that there is some remaining purity that is not produced by the sublime contemplations?
One must understand that the three contemplations are taught precisely because they are intended to give rise to the purity of the Shared Land.

This is truly because the contemplation of the subtle can destroy the three delusions; it does not merely lead to rebirth in the Pure Land of Common Residence, but according to the depth or shallowness of the delusions severed, one naturally attains the three [Pure Lands], such as the Land of Remainder and so forth.

Just as one who is ill requires medicine primarily for the sake of physical recovery, yet upon obtaining and compounding a prescription from an immortal, not only does the body recover but the bones also become light;
the recovery of the body may be likened to being born in the Land of Shared Purity, while the lightness of the bones may be likened to attaining the three higher lands.
However, there is one medicine whose efficacy is profoundly superior, just as a single sublime contemplation can purify the four lands.

The *Awakening of Faith* states that when a beginner practices the Mahāyāna with right faith, they fear that in this land they will not always encounter a Buddha and may thus lose their faith; therefore, it teaches them to seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, instructing them to contemplate that Buddha’s Tathatā-dharmakāya, so that they will ultimately attain birth and abide in the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
If one does not possess the three perfect contemplations, how can one illumine the Dharmakāya?
How then can it be said that the cause of Sukhāvatī consists solely of mundane wholesome deeds?
Fourth, the discussion of its function.
The "principle" (zong) refers to the Dharma cultivated for one's own practice; the "application" (yong) refers to the Dharma bestowed for the benefit of others.

Because one's own practice proceeds toward the ultimate principle, it clarifies wondrous contemplation; because transforming others involves gathering sentient beings, it encompasses all manner of wholesome deeds.
He should skillfully contemplate this and must also be taught to cultivate the auxiliary practices for his own realization; how could he ever abandon the various virtues?
Therefore, while the fundamental principle and the application of the Dharma must be equal, there is only the distinction between practicing for oneself and transforming others.
The text has two parts:
first, the title and brief indication.
Because power possesses function, it is called "powerful function" (*liyòng*).
What is the function of power?
It is to give rise to the good and extinguish evil.
A practitioner should understand these three aspects: essence, doctrine, and function.

To clarify the three dharmas separately: they arise from the one nature into two practices. Their essence is the nature manifested by the *dharmakāya*; their principle is the wisdom manifested by *prajñā*; and their function is the power arising from *vimukti*.
Although the second is accomplished through cultivation, one must know it to be inherently complete;
although the first is the fundamental nature, it arises entirely to constitute cultivation.
Therefore, they are neither sequential nor simultaneous, and are inconceivable.
The two virtues reside within the nature; they refer entirely to afflictions and karma, which are precisely the two cultivated virtues of good and evil inherently possessed by the nature.

Now, when one embodies these contrary cultivations, because they are fully inherent in the nature, their fusion and subtlety at that very locus constitute the virtue of transforming others. Therefore, these two are taken as the primary function of the Sūtra’s central doctrine.
It is employed universally; it is not that there is no application for evil, for by conforming to its nature, it gives rise to the wholesome and extinguishes the unwholesome.
Therefore, when applied to defiled and evil applications, employing it in accordance with its nature is most capable of extinguishing evil.
Below "Eliminating Evil," there is a broad explanation based on its meaning, divided into two parts.
First, a comprehensive clarification regarding both good and evil:
since the application of power necessarily accomplishes meritorious virtue, a single function thus possesses four names.

To argue one-sidedly that the eradication of evil requires the exertion of effort, and to argue one-sidedly that the production of goodness resides in virtuous function—this is merely a preliminary view.

From a second perspective, however, both power and function, as well as merit and virtue, are capable of eradicating evil; and both power and function, as well as merit and virtue, are capable of producing goodness.

One must know that the eradication of evil reaches its ultimate limit at Avīci Hell, while the cultivation of goodness logically culminates in the state of Subtle Enlightenment (Miaojue); only then does one realize the power, function, and merit of this Perfect Sūtra.
Second, from the phrase "Suffering is... onwards, there is a partial explanation regarding the eradication of evil, in two parts:
first, there is no evil that is not eliminated.
Regarding what is called the extinction of evil: one must extinguish the causes of evil in order to eliminate its effects.

If practitioners who cultivate either the fruit or the cause do not eradicate the three poisons—the root of all suffering—then even if they temporarily escape suffering, it will never be permanently ended.
Now, it is explained that by practicing the contemplation of the Pure Land for the sake of transforming others, one causes both the causes and effects of all evils to be extinguished.
Even if delusions have not yet been severed, they will not arise upon birth there; since their severance is imminent, one is able to eternally extinguish evil causes and evil effects.
To state it briefly, the power and function of this sutra extinguish the causes of the five abodes and eliminate the fruits of the two deaths.
Second, from the words "Therefore," below, it is explained through further detailed distinctions.

Among the gravest evils, none surpasses the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*); these are karmic actions arising from the highest grade of afflictions that bring about the sufferings of the Avīci hell.
The great power of this sutra can extinguish such extremely heavy threefold obstacles, leading one to be born immediately in the Pure Land.
If these three obstacles are by nature not the same as the three virtues, how could they be transformed without interval into supreme bliss?
Starting from those of the most dull faculties, let us consider that ten recitations may give rise to the lowest grade;
yet for those of sharp faculties, it is not impossible to give rise to the eight higher grades.
Because the essence of the five heinous offenses is the land of serene light, one may thereby purify these four Buddha-lands.
Fifth, the classification of the characteristics of the teachings:
the teaching consists of the words of the Sages addressed to those below.
"Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) refer to the formal marks that can be distinguished upon examination.
The four preceding meanings are all verbal teachings—that is, teachings that express through names.

These are the teachings that express the essence, the tenet, and the function. If one distinguishes them by way of their characteristics, it causes the reader to perceive them with clarity; therefore, their characteristics are demonstrated according to the five periods, the two treasuries, and the gradual and sudden approaches.

Among the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles, this belongs to the Mahāyāna.
Although within the sūtras there are instances where individuals such as Piṇḍola attain the Lesser Vehicle, they are not the primary intended recipients of this specific teaching.

Now, as for preaching the contemplations of the Pure Land for Vaidehī and others according to the definitive teaching, these are neither merely general nor specific; how could they possibly belong to the Hīnayāna?
Among the five periods of the Buddha's teaching, this belongs to the third period, that of the Shared Teaching (Vaipulya).

For now, the characteristics of the texts are analyzed, while the distinction between the settled (*ding*) and the dispersed (*san*) has not yet been discussed.
Second, the classification according to the two baskets (*piṭaka*).
When the Dharma is categorized according to the individuals for whom it is intended, this belongs to the Bodhisattvas.
Although the *Āgama* and other sūtras speak of the Three Vehicles, they belong to the Śrāvaka Piṭaka from the perspective of their majority and their primary focus.

Although the various schools of the Mahāyāna include both the Two Vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha), these are not the primary intent of those schools; therefore, the classification of the Piṭakas is attributed to the Bodhisattvas.
Third, regarding the gradual and sudden:

if one discusses the gradual and sudden according to the pedagogical methods of conversion (*saṃdarśana-vidhi*), the *Avataṃsaka* belongs to the sudden, while the three periods [of the Buddha’s teaching] all belong to the gradual.
The sutra exists within the Vaipulya (fangděng) class, yet it is not "sudden" in terms of the pedagogical method (*huà-yí*).

What is "sudden" in this present sutra refers to the suddenness of the perfect (*yuán*) nature within the teachings of transformation (*huà-fǎ*); therefore, based on the fact that Vimalakīrti attained patience (*kṣānti*) in his very body, the classification of the teaching is determined as sudden.

Furthermore, regarding the stage of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), it is distinctively attained at the first ground (*bhūmi*) and perfectly realized at the first dwelling (*vihāra*).

In the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna-śāsana*), ordinary beings must pass through incalculable eons before reaching this stage; only in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) can one enter it in this very life.

If one were to judge the partiality or completeness of the teachings based on the benefits conferred by their conferral, it would be most evident; therefore, in this present text, the teaching is determined according to the practitioner's capacity and stage of realization as being sudden and not gradual.
Second, under the heading "Title," the speaker is briefly distinguished.
If four persons were to speak and the Tathāgata validated it, it too could be called a *sūtra*.
Since this present *sūtra* was spoken from the golden mouth [of the Buddha] from beginning to end, it is titled "Spoken by the Buddha."
Second, "Analysis of the Text" (*fenwen*) follows the sūtra to clarify its meaning.
Previously, the five meanings—name and so forth—were taken from within the sūtra to explain the general title.

Although the overall intent has been made manifest, the specific textual details remain difficult to discern; therefore, it is necessary to demarcate the sūtra’s sentences and sections so that the meaning may be clearly revealed.

Although the general and specific [aspects] differ, their meaning does not diverge into two paths; thus one comes to know that the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) explains the title of this sutra, and further understands that the sentences of the commentary do not manifest any other meaning.
