First, the Introductory Section (Jōbun) has two parts:
First is the Preface of Right Faith, which is the General Preface.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When the Buddha was about to enter nirvana, Ānanda asked the Buddha:
'What words should be placed at the beginning of all sūtras?'"
The Buddha answered Ānanda:
"One should say: 'Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was at a certain place in a certain land, together with a certain great assembly.'"
"It is not only in my own teaching that this is so; it was likewise at the beginning of the sutras of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Thus we know that these six meanings constitute the general introduction (sādhāraṇa-nidāna), for they are common to all sutras.
It is also called the "preface" because it was entrusted [to the assembly] for their preservation;
it is also called the "postscript" because it was placed there by the compilers.
What is now termed "testimony of faith" is intended to ensure that those who hear it do not harbor doubts.
Treatise, Question Four:
Why not speak directly of *prajñā* (wisdom), rather than saying [the Buddha] "dwelt in Rājagṛha"?
Answer:
The mention of time, place, and person is for the purpose of inspiring faith in others.
As for the term "six phrases," a phrase is defined simply as that which completes the expression of a meaning.
For example, even a single word spoken by the Buddha is termed a phrase.
2. First, the six phrases indicating the heading.
Regarding "Thus indicating faith," the second question in the *Śāstra* asks:
For what reason do the sūtras of all Buddhas begin with the words "Thus" (*evam*)?
Answer:
The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma is entered through faith and crossed by means of wisdom.
Such a principle is precisely what constitutes faith.
If a person possesses faith, they can enter the Buddha-dharma; without faith, they cannot enter.
One who lacks faith says that such a matter is not so, while one who has faith says that such a matter is indeed so.
"I have heard from another non-Buddhist" (I have heard from a different outsider): because he personally received [the teaching] from the Buddha, he says "I have heard.
This distinguishes him from the non-Buddhists, who did not receive the Buddha's instruction.
"At one time, when disputes were stilled": this refers to the moment when the disciples' faculties were matured and they received the Way; therefore, there was no dispute.
The *Śāstra* states: "It cannot be that there is not even one [Buddha] at a time.
The Buddha himself said:
'When one person appears in the world, many people obtain happiness.'"
"Who is this person?
It is the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Second, from "Thus" onwards, the meaning is explained according to the text, in six parts:
First, the indication of faith.
Faith is defined as endurance and delight.
Logically, it should be called "wholesome," for only when one endures and delights can it truly be so.
When principle accords with reality, it is not different; this is called "Thus" (tathā).
When words are good, they are without error; this is called "Right" (samyak).
The teachings of the four vehicles all refer to principle as "Thus" (evam), yet there are differences in their depth and shallowness.
If it concerns the Tripitaka, it speaks only of non-difference and non-exclusion from the perspective of conventional truth;
although the comprehensive teaching (Tongjiao) identifies with principle, it remains within the two truths;
whereas in the knowledge of the Middle Way according to the Separate Teaching (Biejiao), one must first break through the two [truths].

Only the Perfect [Teaching] allows the beginner to immediately realize that within each and every phenomenon there is reality, and that in its very place it is suchness; speaking in accordance with this, there is nothing that is not "is.
Therefore, when compared to the three teachings, none of them are like this.

Although the faith in this sutra has not yet been opened or discarded, the capacities it addresses do not follow the partial or limited [teachings of the Hinayana]; therefore, one can decisively believe in its suchness as it is perfectly and fully revealed.
Since this first phrase is thus, the intent of the following five phrases all lies in the Perfect [Teaching].
Therefore, while the general preface is common [to all teachings] and its meaning is also common, their specific intents are distinct.
Now, I shall explain this general text with a specific intention; hence these words are spoken.
Second, from "Thus have I heard" onwards, [the section] distinguishing [this teaching] from that of the non-Buddhists has two parts:
first, the direct explanation.
The phrase "there was" (asti) refers to the Buddha.
Although it explains "I heard," its intent primarily clarifies the act of hearing;
the subsequent passage then clarifies the "I."
Second, from "As for 'I'" onwards, there is a critical examination in two parts:
first, the formulation of an objection.
"I" carries the meaning of being autonomous and possessing sovereignty.

Ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle are attached to a self within persons and phenomena; now, the Perfect Contemplation is transmitted as being in accord with the two types of emptiness—how then can one speak of a "self"?
Second, from "Conforming to the World" onwards, the general resolution of the objection has two parts:
first, the direct resolution.
Although a self cannot be found within ultimate emptiness, this very emptiness is the conventional reality, wherein all selves are manifest.
For now, let us distinguish the characteristics of the self according to three types:

the "view-self," which is the imputed notion of a sovereign controller; the "pride-self," which is the innate sense of a sovereign controller; and the "nominal self," which follows worldly convention.

When the Venerable Ānanda reached the time of the First Council, he had already shattered the "self" of the pride of identity-view; how then could there be two kinds of self within the realm of conditioned existence?
It was for the sake of propagation and transformation that he conformed to the conventional truth and established the designation of a "self."
2. From "Just as a person" onwards, an analogy is presented.
Knowing the principle of non-self is like using gold coins;
establishing a self in accordance with worldly convention is like exchanging them for copper coins, wood, grass, and so forth.
III. From "First" onwards, the settling of disputes is analyzed in two parts:
first, the presentation of the commentary; second, the explanation of the first [point]. Within the first part, there is the explanation of the first [point].
First, [the text] refutes [the position] based on ultimate truth; second, it establishes [it] according to conventional truth—this can be seen in the text itself.

Regarding the "Extensive Refutation of Identity and Difference" in the *Śāstra*, the treatise states: "If [identity] were one with the thing, or if [identity] were different from the thing, both cases would entail faults."
Question:
If they were one, what fault would there be? Answer:
If they were one, then "one" would have the same meaning as "vase.
Since "one" exists everywhere, every place should be a vase, and consequently, there would be no such things as clothing and so forth.
Such being the fault in the case of oneness, what of the fault in the case of twoness?
Answer:
If "one" were different from the jar, then the jar would not be one.
If the jar were different from "one," then "one" would not be the jar.
If the pot and the "one" were conjoined such that the pot was named "one," then why, when the "one" is now conjoined with the pot, is the "one" not named the pot?
Therefore, one cannot say that the pot is different from the "one."
That passage is extremely extensive.
Since a jar is manifest and visible, it is used as a metaphor for time.
Furthermore, "one" is a number, whereas time is a substantial entity (dravya).

If one dogmatically adheres to the identity or difference of the substance of number, then all delusions will arise in confusion; however, one who can abandon such adherence is liberated regarding phenomena (*dharma*).

This, by relying on the single principle of the substance of number, demonstrates the contemplation of detachment, causing one to eliminate fixed calculations regarding all phenomena. Thus, it should be known that the six matters as well as all other texts require the abandonment of views concerning identity and difference.
2. Explanation of "Time" (*kāla*).

In this land [China], when designating and summoning it, one simply says "time. In India, there are two pronunciations: if one says *kāla*, it refers to actual time; if one says *samaya*, it refers to conventional time.

It is also like how, in this world, the mind has two designations: "wisdom" (jñāna) refers to the mind of understanding, while "consciousness" (vijñāna) refers to the deluded mind; therefore, one is instructed to rely on wisdom and not on consciousness.
Non-Buddhists (bāhyaka) grasp time as a real cause; therefore, in contrast to them, it is called *samaya* to reveal that time is conventional (*prajñapti*).
If a follower of our own school (ādhyātmika) eats according to the time, observes the rules of purity (*vidyāmātra*), and so forth, they speak of *kāla*, revealing that time is real (*dravya*).
Regarding the statement that *kṣaṇa* (moment) is a short duration and *tatsamaya* (that-time) is a long duration: according to the treatises, both short and long durations are termed *tatsamaya*.

This refers to names such as direction, time, conjunction and disjunction, unity and difference, length and shortness; these arise from the attachments of ordinary people. Therefore, both long and short are merely conventional designations and lack substantial reality.

Regarding the current division of "short" and "long" corresponding to these two names, I suspect that the Great Master, relying on the gate of provisional establishment (*prajñapti-mukha*), skillfully harmonized the intent of the treatise: namely, that according to the Buddha’s system of time, the duration of birth and death is short, whereas according to the non-Buddhists' adherence to [cyclical] time, the duration of birth and death is long; since he has reinterpreted the treatise's text, this must certainly have been his underlying intention.
2. From "Now, not... onwards, the present intention is clarified.
Regarding the phrase "not discussed," etc.: here, it is not a matter of protecting the marks and signs within the realm; therefore, actual time is not discussed.
Furthermore, this is not a time for refuting external attachments that take time to be real; therefore, conventional time is not discussed.
The length [of the discourse] is as previously stated.
It is simply that when the faculties (*indriya*) of sentient beings have matured, the Buddha should preach the sutra.
The moment when the faculty and the response coincide is also the moment when the truth (*satya*) and wisdom (*jñāna*) coincide; therefore, it is called "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*).
The text merely follows what was appropriate, hence it says "preaching the sutra.
How could the Buddha preach the Dharma in vain without sentient beings responding with spiritual resonance?
Therefore, once the Buddha had finished preaching and Vaidehī had completed her realization.

However, while the words and meanings of this passage are fundamentally applicable to both the shallow and the profound levels, the present intention specifically concerns the response of the Buddha to those with the capacity for the Perfect Teaching (*yuanji*), thereby enabling ordinary beings to enter directly into the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).
Fourth, from the phrase "The Buddha" onwards, the subject of transformation is treated in three parts;
first, an explanation based on alternative names.
In the fourth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the term Bhagavat is explained through four meanings:
first, the ability to destroy afflictions;
second, the possession of merit.
Third, skillful discernment, because he is able to discern the general and specific characteristics of all phenomena;
fourth, excellent renown, because there is no one who has attained fame and reputation equal to that of the Buddha.
The current text briefly sets forth two meanings, while the new [translation] states that Bhagavat possesses six meanings:
first, sovereignty; second, brilliance; third, majesty; fourth, renown; fifth, auspiciousness; and sixth, nobility.
Because it contains many meanings, it is not translated; the old rendering "Bhagavān" is a corruption.
Second, from "As for 'Buddha'" below, the term is explained by way of the three types of awakening.
From "As for 'Buddha'" below, there is a general indication.
From "Furthermore, it can... onwards, there is a specific exposition.
Third is Awakening (*bodhi*).

In relation to delusion, it is called self-awakening; in relation to the self, it is called other-awakening; in relation to the cause, it is called perfect awakening. These three distinct aspects of the one equal awakening are spoken of as the three types of awakening.
Third, from "All" downward, the explanation is given by way of transcending causes:
because of all-knowledge, he differs from the heterodox and their delusions;
because of objectless compassion, he differs from the Hinayanists who seek only their own deliverance.
Because the three types of wisdom are equal, it differs from the various bodhisattvas;
because it is ultimate awakening, it differs from all causal stages.
Its capacity to differ is not distinct [from its essence], as this is defined in relation to that which it differs from.
4. Four types of discrimination.
However, regarding the explanation of the meaning of "Buddha," the six identities (*liù jí*) and so forth explain the text somewhat in detail; therefore, I shall now speak of it briefly.
5. From "Those who abide" (*zài zhě*) onwards, the treatise discusses the place of abiding, in two parts:
First, the explanation of "abiding" has two parts:
first, the assembly abides together.
To categorize this as "temporary abiding" versus "long-term abiding" is merely a provisional distinction and does not exhaust the full meaning of the principle.
Whether one dwells for a long time or stays but briefly, what hindrance could there be?
Moreover, since the Nirmāṇakāya of the Tathāgata constantly resides within Vulture Peak Mountain, how can it be said that he stays only temporarily?
2. From "The one who abides" (*sthātṛ*) onwards, the commentary explains "abiding" (*sthiti*).

This sutra uses the term "being present" (*vartamāna*), while the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* uses "abiding" (*sthita*); since their meanings do not differ, this commentary cites the meaning of "abiding" from that treatise to explain "being present."
This is divided into two parts.
First, the enumeration:
"The four modes of deportment" refers to walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.
These bodily postures are all situated on Vulture Peak, yet there are four distinctions in the ways one abides in the Dharma: namely, the celestial, the Brahma-like, the noble, and the Buddha-like.
Second, "The Celestial Abode" (devasthāna) and below provide the explanation.

The current passage concerning the four abidings (*catur-vihāra*) is actually a complete extraction of the treatise’s explanation of the meaning of "abiding. Thus, we know that within these four, both cause and fruit are clarified; however, that which truly constitutes the ability to abide lies precisely in the cause.

That which is called the Tathāgata’s manifestation of giving, morality, and the ten wholesome mental states for the sake of gathering sentient beings—this is the Buddha dwelling in Rājagṛha by means of the dharmas of the desire-realm heavens;

for the sake of sentient beings, he manifests the four immeasurable minds and the three samādhis, which is the dwelling in Rājagṛha and other cities by means of the Brahma-dharmas and the noble dharmas.
These are all instances of the Tathāgata dwelling in accordance with the intentions of others.
If he were to dwell according to his own intention, he would immediately proceed from the *Śūraṅgama* Samādhi through to the *Asādhāraṇa* (Unshared) Samādhi and so forth to reside in the Royal City.
Therefore, the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra* states: "Śākyamuni is named Vairocana; the dwelling place of this Buddha is called the Constantly Quiescent Light."

Since Śākyamuni and Vairocana are alternative names, and the Royal City and the Land of Quiescent Light are ultimately non-dual, it is said that this Buddha’s dwelling place is named "Eternal Quiescence."
What kind of realm is that in which one currently dwells?

Furthermore, one should understand that if one distinguishes between subject and object in terms of persons and dharmas, then everything from generosity and morality up to the Śūraṅgama-samādhi and so forth are the dharmas in which one dwells, while the Buddha is the one who dwells therein.
If one takes the royal city as the place of residence, those of superior status are all termed "able to dwell.
Furthermore, since the scriptural text simply states "the Buddha dwells," the treatise should explain it solely in terms of the Śūraṅgama-samādhi;
yet, regarding the clarification of the first three [samādhis], Jingxi offers two interpretations:
First, it proceeds from the general toward the particular, moving from the broad to the narrow.
Second, it subsumes the inferior by means of the superior; since the Buddha resides in the royal city, he necessarily encompasses those of the desire and form realms, as well as the three vehicles.
Since the Buddha’s abiding is supreme, there is no dharma that does not abide within it;
yet, it is not that he does not abide in evil—for the sake of attracting sentient beings, he provisionally speaks from the perspective of the wholesome.

Within the wholesome, he briefly designates mundane goodness as "heaven" and "Brahmā," thereby subsuming all forms of wholesome states, whether concentrated or scattered. Thus, he speaks of heaven and Brahmā.
Within the supramundane, the "holy Buddha" is briefly indicated as encompassing all phenomena through the categories of the Small and Great Vehicles; thus, he is called "Holy.

Others do not understand that the mind-dharma can abide [therein], but merely say that his body dwelt in Rājagṛha and so forth; this suppresses the ultimate Sage by equating his dwelling with that of ordinary beings.

Moreover, both ordinary beings and sages each possess the dharmas by which they abide; for instance, when a bhikṣu cultivates morality, concentration, and wisdom, he dwells in his quarters by means of the celestial, Brahma, and noble abodes.
If one violates the precepts, then hell shall dwell within their quarters.
If one is able to cultivate the three contemplations with single-mindedness, then the very place where they reside is itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.
Is it not the case that the *Śūraṅgama* is the dharma in which one dwells?
If even those at the initial stage of practice are thus, how can it be said that a Buddha in fruition dwells only in his body?

first, the explanation of the city; in two parts:
first, the transliteration of the Sanskrit name.
It is also called Magadha, which means "Non-Harming.
This refers to the fact that the laws of this country do not employ corporal punishment; those who commit crimes punishable by death are sent to the Śītavana (Cold Forest).
Second, "The Commentary" below provides an explanation in three parts:

Regarding the phrase "Śrīmālā" and so forth: Śrīmālā was the Lady Śrīmālā, the daughter of King Prasenajit of Śrāvastī and born of Queen Mallikā; she served as the consort of the King of Ujjayinī.
Subsequently, her parents sent a letter stating: "A Buddha has appeared in our country; his supernormal powers are sovereign, and he universally benefits all sentient beings.
Vaśiṣṭhā took the letter and, addressing the messenger, spoke this verse:
"I reverently contemplate the World-Honored Buddha, who has appeared for the sake of the entire world; may he likewise take pity on us and come swiftly to this place."
As soon as these verses were spoken, the Buddha manifested in the air.
He further spoke in verse of praise, saying:

Now, as Vaidehī’s piteous plea was made, the Buddha immediately descended to her; since the circumstances were similar, it is said that they are "not different. Second, regarding the section beginning with "Knowing Vaidehī," there is a sequential explanation in five parts; first, the supernormal powers (ṛddhi), which has two sub-sections: 1. The Buddha’s descent to Vaidehī’s palace. 2. The manifestation of the Pure Land. First, the Buddha’s descent to Vaidehī’s palace: The Buddha, knowing that Vaidehī had been imprisoned by her son Ajātaśatru, immediately manifested his great supernatural power (*maharddhibala*). He transformed the iron city into lapis lazuli, the iron walls into crystal, and the iron moats into fragrant water. He caused the palace to appear like a jeweled pavilion, adorned with various precious ornaments. Then, he entered the palace through the eastern gate, proceeded to the central hall, and sat upon a lion throne. At that time, the king of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, along with eighty-four thousand devas, also arrived at the palace and stood to one side. The Buddha then addressed Vaidehī: "Why do you weep so bitterly? She replied: "My son Ajātaśatru has imprisoned me in this iron city, intending to starve me to death. Therefore, I weep. The Buddha said: "Do not fear. I shall now lead you to see Amitābha Buddha and his land of Sukhāvatī. Having spoken thus, he extended his right hand and stroked her head three times. Instantly, she felt as though she had ascended to the Tuṣita Heaven. The Buddha then took her by the hand and led her out of the palace. As they emerged from the eastern gate, they saw a great jeweled pond filled with pure water, its bottom covered in golden sand, and adorned with seven rows of jewel trees. The Buddha then led her to the shore of the pond and sat down. At that moment, the earth shook in six ways, and the entire assembly saw the Buddha’s body transform into a hundred thousand *koṭis* of bodies, each body emitting sixty *koṭis* of rays of light. From each ray of light issued sixty *koṭis* of transformation Buddhas, and from each transformation Buddha issued sixty *koṭis* of transformation bodhisattvas. All these transformation Buddhas and bodhisattvas rose into the air and proceeded toward the west. After traveling for ten thousand *yojanas*, they reached a place where they saw a great jeweled pond. From within the pond, they heard the sound of music, and from the sky above, they heard the sounds of singing and dancing. The Buddha then told Vaidehī: "That is the land of Sukhāvatī, where the Tathāgata Amitābha dwells. He further explained: "In that land, there is no suffering such as birth, old age, sickness, or death. There are only birds, trees, and ponds that spontaneously produce the sounds of the Dharma. Those who hear them will naturally give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). Having finished speaking, the Buddha withdrew his hand, and the transformation bodies all vanished. The Buddha then took Vaidehī by the hand and led her back into the palace. At that time, the king of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven and the eighty-four thousand devas all followed the Buddha into the palace and stood to one side. The Buddha then addressed Vaidehī: "Would you like to see the land of Sukhāvatī? She replied: "I would like to see it. The Buddha then extended his right hand and stroked her head three times. Instantly, she saw the land of Sukhāvatī, the Buddha Amitābha, and the assembly of bodhisattvas. Having seen them, her mind became joyful and serene, and she attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*). This is called the first part: the Buddha’s descent to Vaidehī’s palace. Second, the manifestation of the Pure Land: The Buddha then addressed Vaidehī: "The land of Sukhāvatī is vast and boundless, adorned with the seven treasures, and filled with lotus flowers. It is free from the sufferings of the three evil realms. There are only birds, trees, and ponds that spontaneously produce the sounds of the Dharma. Those who hear them will naturally give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment. Furthermore, in that land, there is no sun or moon; the light of the Buddha’s body illuminates everywhere, and the light of the bodhisattvas also shines universally. There is no distinction between day and night. The ground is made of gold, and the trees are made of the seven treasures. The birds are born from the Buddha’s transformation to preach the Dharma and lead sentient beings to liberation. The water in the ponds is clear and pure, with eight virtues. Within the water grow various lotuses, some as large as a chariot wheel, others as large as a city, and others as large as a mountain. Each flower emits a hundred thousand *koṭis* of rays of light, and from each ray of light issue transformation Buddhas. These transformation Buddhas preach the Dharma for sentient beings, causing them to attain liberation. In that land, there is no suffering such as hunger or thirst; those who wish to eat or drink need only think of it, and their bowls will be filled. When they have finished eating, the bowls will vanish on their own. There are also jeweled curtains and canopies, and the fragrance of incense pervades everywhere. The bodhisattvas there are of two kinds: those born from the womb and those born by transformation. Those born from the womb are like the bodhisattva Maitreya, who was born from the right side of Queen Māyā. Those born by transformation are like the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and the bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, who were born by transformation from a lotus flower. In that land, there is no womanhood; even those who are women in this world will, upon being reborn there, become men. There is no suffering of birth, old age, sickness, or death. Even if one has committed the five grave offenses or the ten evil deeds, if one hears the name of Amitābha Buddha and, with a sincere heart, recites it ten times, one will be reborn in that land. Even those who have committed the four grave offenses or the five heinous crimes, if they hear the name of Amitābha Buddha and, with a sincere heart, recite it ten times, they will not fall into the three evil realms but will be reborn in that land. In that land, there is no retrogression; once reborn there, one will surely attain Buddhahood. Having finished speaking, the Buddha withdrew his hand, and the vision of the Pure Land vanished. This is called the second part: the manifestation of the Pure Land. Third, the teaching of the Dharma to Vaidehī. Fourth, Vaidehī’s attainment of the stage of non-retrogression. Fifth, the Buddha’s departure from the palace. Third, the teaching of the Dharma to Vaidehī: The Buddha then addressed Vaidehī: "If you wish to be reborn in the land of Sukhāvatī, you must cultivate the three minds and practice the three practices. What are the three minds? First, the mind of deep faith (*adhimukti*), which means believing that the Buddha’s lands are real and that one can indeed be reborn there. Second, the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), which means pitying all sentient beings and wishing to deliver them all. Third, the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), which means dedicating all roots of goodness toward rebirth in that land. What are the three practices? First, the practice of good conduct (*śīla*), which means observing the precepts purely and not violating them. Second, the practice of concentration (*samādhi*), which means practicing meditation and attaining various samādhis. Third, the practice of wisdom (*prajñā*), which means studying the teachings of the Buddha and attaining the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). If you can cultivate these three minds and three practices, you will certainly be reborn in the land of Sukhāvatī. Vaidehī then asked: "What are the names of the Buddhas of the ten directions? The Buddha replied: "They are Akṣobhya Buddha, Amitābha Buddha, Ratnasaṃbhava Buddha, Sarvalokadhātūpadravodvegapratyuttīrṇa Buddha, Sarvārthasiddha Buddha, Sarvaguṇaviśeṣasamudgata Buddha, Sarvadharmaprabhāsa Buddha, Sarvajagadrakṣa Buddha, Sarvabuddhaviṣayāvatāra-jñāna Buddha, and Sarvabuddhadharmasamudra-vyavalokana-samādhi-rāja Buddha. These are the names of the Buddhas of the ten directions. You should single-mindedly take refuge

It is through the contemplation of an aspiration that the causal condition for karma is established.

This request concerns the practice that effectively assists the path.

the act of apprehending an object of focus is termed "right reception" (*samyag-samādhi*).
This is the request for the World-Honored One to teach the method of practicing the visualization of the Pure Land, which is precisely *samyag-darśana* (correct observation).

Regarding the phrase "the beginner shares with ordinary beings" and so forth: these three kinds of merit are now the complete aids to the Path; because they are conjoined with right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), they are all the practices of the Tathāgata. However, because these three types of existence are both general and specific: the first, filial support and so forth, is common to both the Mahayana and Hinayana, as well as to ordinary persons at the stage of broad cultivation; therefore, it is said that "the first practice is shared with ordinary beings."
Next, the precepts and so forth apply exclusively to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; since ordinary beings have no share in them, it is said that "next, they are shared with the Two Vehicles.

2. Regarding the section beginning with "The commentary says," there are two points in the response.

First, because of the Buddha’s power, those who practice contemplation are enabled to see immediately upon wishing to do so; thus this text states, "You should fix your mindfulness and contemplate that land with clarity. Therefore, we know that the Buddha’s power assists those who wish to see, enabling their contemplation to result in vision.
The subsequent text states: "All sentient beings contemplate the Western World of Ultimate Bliss; by the power of the Buddha, they shall behold that pure land."
Therefore, the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi-sūtra* speaks of three powers when one beholds the Buddha:
first, the power of the Buddha; second, the power of samādhi; and third, the power of the practitioner’s own fundamental merit.
Next, "the mind" refers to the manifestation of lands within light, which is to say, seeing them with one's own eyes.
Both of these types of vision arise from the principle of resonance and response; thus, although distant, they are near.

However, if the nature of the mind did not inherently contain the dust-motes and lands, then there would be no principle for the Buddhas to manifest in response, nor would sentient beings possess the capacity to perceive through resonance. Therefore, this sutra declares that "this mind is Buddha."
To observe this intention as being deluded would not constitute the sublime tenet.

Provided that the mind which practices is in each instance in accord with the true nature (dharmatā), what prevents the wholesome deeds of practicing compassion and filial piety from being shared with ordinary beings?

Regarding matters such as the Three Refuges, the various precepts, and dignified deportment, it is simply that the mind with which one upholds them accords with the One Body and relies upon the ultimate reality, while the dharmas practiced therein are common to the Two Vehicles.

Raising a vow without an object based on the realm of non-action is called the arousal of the bodhicitta.
Although the true mark is non-dual, it appears as dual, establishing the distinction between cause and fruit.
Duality is non-duality; from beginning to end, the principle is one.
To have faith in this cause and effect is what is truly called "profound.

To read and recite the Mahāyāna, to cultivate the understanding of the three wisdoms, and to carry out the practice of the Perfect Vehicle—teaching practitioners through such understanding and practice—is called "exhortation and encouragement."

Regarding these three types of karma: one who attains the former does not necessarily attain the latter, whereas one who attains the latter necessarily attains the former. Thus, while practitioners today may be able to cultivate the first two, those two cannot cultivate the Mahāyāna; therefore, it is said that "the other two do not equal this, which refers to the Mahāyāna."

Since this is the work of the Buddha, it is verified as the practice of perfect cultivation; thus, in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, there is another category of conduct called the "Tathāgata Conduct."
Although it is said that there is but one practice, it actually encompasses five practices.
Now it is the same here: although this is the work of the Buddha, it nonetheless comprises three types.

Regarding the phrase "Listen attentively" (*śṛṇuta*), such injunctions appear in all sutras; there are none that do not cause listeners to give rise to the three types of wisdom (*trividya*).

However, one must examine the teachings to clarify whether these wisdoms are partial or complete, as well as the relationship between the listener and the taught, the thinker and the thought, and the rememberer and the remembered.
If one forms an understanding of arising and ceasing, this refers to the three wisdoms of the Tripitaka.
An understanding of non-arising refers to the three wisdoms of the Shared Teaching.
The immeasurable and the unconditioned (wu zuo) can be understood as belonging to the Distinct and Perfect Teachings.
Now, [the Buddha] causes Vaidehī and the others to give rise to the threefold perfect wisdom; were it not so, how could they realize the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti) in this very seat?
Third, from "immediately attained" onwards, there is a brief entrustment to Ānanda.

Regarding the passage beginning with "As if holding a bright mirror," one contemplates phenomena as being like a mirror and cultivates them as if holding it; when contemplation is perfected, the land appears, just as one sees the reflection of a face.
Thus we know that one must possess the three kinds of pure karma externally and be fully equipped with the sixteen sublime contemplations internally before one can see [the Buddha].
Although this briefly mentions pure karma, its underlying intent is to explain the sublime contemplations.

Regarding the phrase "the first dwelling in the first stage": both the Perfect [Teaching] and the Distinct [Teaching] break through ignorance at this point; this is the stage of *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena).

The *Myōgen* (Miaoxuan), in its section on the "Single Reality Stage," states: "If one enters the first dwelling, one is precisely breaking through ignorance; this is the stage of *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* in the Perfect Teaching. My intention here lies in the Perfect Teaching.
The citation of the five stages of patience (*kṣānti*) from the *Renwang jing* serves to demonstrate that the stage of non-arising (*anutpāda*) resides above the three patiences.

According to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), these are: the Patience of Subjugation during the ten faiths (*śraddhā*), the Patience of Faith during the ten abidings (*vihāra*), the Patience of Accordance during the ten practices (*caryā*), the Patience of Non-Arising during the ten grounds (*bhūmi*), and the Patience of Quiescent Extinction at the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

If categorized according to the stages of perfection: the five grades of subduing patience (*vinaya-kṣānti*) constitute the purity of the six sense faculties; the two patiences of faith and compliance (*śraddhā-anukūla-kṣānti*) extend from the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) up to equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), which is termed the patience of non-arising (*anutpāda-kṣānti*); and the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*) is termed the patience of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa-kṣānti*).
However, the first bhūmi is identical to the first perfect dwelling; therefore, the *Renyō-kyō* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) is cited to authenticate this present stage.

Practitioners should know that as the Tathāgata was about to expound the method of the sixteen contemplations, he prefigured that what was to be taught was the perfectly wondrous contemplation; thus he said: "If all sentient beings contemplate the Land of Ultimate Bliss, once the contemplation is perfected, they shall immediately attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."

Therefore, when Vaidehī heard the teaching on the sixteen visualizations, she accomplished them according to the words; as soon as the exposition was finished, she immediately realized this sublime stage.
The Sūtra demonstrates that these visualizations are the direct and swift gateway to entering the first *bhūmi*; thus, they cannot be said to be merely conceptualizations of objects.

II. From "First Explanation" onwards, there is the explanation of the sixteen subtle contemplations as the answer to the correct reception (samāpatti), in two parts: first, the division of sections; second, the word-by-word commentary from "You are...
onwards, in two parts: I. Division of Sections. II.
Word-by-word Commentary, in two parts: 1. From "You are... onwards. 2. [The subsequent explanation].
First, clarifying the reason why Vaidehī beheld the land.
Regarding the sutra’s phrase "not yet having attained the divine eye" and so forth, a question is raised:
Aniruddha’s divine eye is the most supreme, yet he sees only the trichiliocosm; [how then could Vaidehī see the Pure Land?]
How could one who has attained the divine eye see the Land of Peaceful Nurturing by traversing hundreds of thousands of billions of lands?
Answer:
This statement does not refer to the divine eye of a Bodhisattva who has attained true realization; it refers to that of the Two Vehicles.
Therefore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, fascicle twenty-two, states: "The pure divine eye attained by a bodhisattva is different from that attained by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Because it is thus distinct, he perceives all the Buddhas currently residing in the worlds of the ten directions simultaneously.
The *Mahā-śāstra* also speaks in this same way.

Regarding the statement "Vaidhṛya is a great bodhisattva," this reveals that Vaidhṛya fundamentally abides in the Dharma-body, yet manifests as an ordinary person in order to inspire the contemplative methods of the Pure Land.
Regarding the phrase "this assembly shall immediately attain the patience of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*): "immediately" (*ji*) here signifies "just about to.

This means that this assembly, upon hearing and contemplating [the teaching], is on the verge of realizing the patience regarding dharmas; it does not mean that the previously mentioned patience of non-arising was realized by Vaidehī.

The preceding passage is a general statement that future sentient beings who cultivate the sixteen contemplations can attain the non-arising of dharmas; yet, seeing the words "manifesting as an ordinary person," some have claimed that the preceding passage refers to Vaidhīya’s own realization.
One should know that this means "will obtain" rather than "has already obtained.

Since they are called true Mahāsattvas, they have long since realized non-arising; it is only from the perspective of their outward manifestations (*traces*) that the Tathāgata says they are ordinary beings with weak and inferior mental conceptions.

Ordinary people of inferior disposition who practice this attain patience; it reveals that this wondrous contemplation can transform base commoners and suddenly bring about the perfection of the sages.
"Extraordinary skillful means" refers to the sixteen contemplative methods, which are extraordinary skillful means.
Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "The sūtras teach an excellent expedient means: by binding the mindfulness [upon] Sukhāvatī, one causes rebirth in that land.

Regarding the phrase "it is not merely contemplating the name that constitutes the expedient means," this means that there are two types of expedient means—concerning both the environment (*bhājanaloka*) and its inhabitants (*sattvaloka*)—which enable ordinary beings of this land to behold it.
First is the skillful means of meditative absorption through the cultivation of contemplation, which causes the mind’s eye to see.
Second is the skillful means of manifestation through the Buddha’s supernormal power, which enables one to witness it with the physical eyes.
Since there are these two ways by which one attains such vision, it is said that "skillful means" does not refer merely to direct observation.
That the Buddha’s power causes one to see is also a skillful means.
Vaidehī thus attains two kinds of vision:
first, the vision that will involve contemplating according to the text; second, the vision granted by the manifestation of the Buddha’s power.
Therefore, it is said: "The reason why Vaidehī saw the land.
Second, from "Vaidehī" onwards, she requests the method for seeing the land for the sake of future generations; this has two parts:
first, the request.
Vaidhīṭī first took the lead, manifesting skillful means as the basis for her request.

Therefore, the Sūtra says, "As I do now, by the power of the Buddha, I see that land"; yet, in formally requesting the skillful means of the method of contemplation, she takes sentient beings as the condition for her request.

Therefore, a sutra says: "If, after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa, all sentient beings are oppressed by the five sufferings of a turbid, evil, and unwholesome age, how shall they behold the World of Ultimate Bliss?"
Regarding the "five sufferings," the commentary provides two interpretations:
first, explaining them as the lack of happiness within the five destinies;

second, explaining them as the retributions summoned by the five transgressions. These are: the suffering of being burned and boiled in hell; the suffering of hunger and thirst among the hungry ghosts; the suffering of slaughter and dismemberment among animals; the eight kinds of suffering in the human realm; and the suffering of the five signs of decline in the heavenly realms.
Regarding the subsequent explanation: the Sage’s intention is manifold; it further clarifies how the five evils invite two types of retribution.
This title appears in the *Mūla-sūtra*, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*; what is now called the "Great Sūtra" (*Dajing*) is this very text.
The commentary first lists the names of the "three" and "five.
Next, from "the five evils" onwards, it explains these three and five categories.
From killing to drinking alcohol, these constitute the causes of the five evils.
The passage beginning with "As in the Great Sūtra" explains the five pains, which are the immediate retributions (*puṣpavipāka*).
The passage beginning with "the five burnings" explains the five burnings, which are the ultimate retributions (*phalavipāka*).
Although these two types of retribution do not each possess five distinct characteristics, they are both designated as "five" because they are established based on five kinds of evil causes.

Therefore, regarding those five items, each subsequent one concludes by stating, "This constitutes one great evil, one pain, and one burning," culminating in the collective statement, "Five great evils, five pains, and five burnings. Thus, we know that both sets of five are established based on their causes.
2. The Response, in two parts:
first, the enumeration of the sections for the analysis of contemplation (kuan), in two parts;
first, the enumeration of the contemplations.
The *Yili* states: "As for the three contemplations (*sanguan*), their meanings are only of three kinds.
The first is 'contemplation according to practice' (*cong xing*), which involves contemplating the one mind within the myriad objects.
Although the myriad objects differ, the principle of the wondrous contemplation is equal; this is precisely the meaning of contemplating the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth."

Second, regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), as in the passages concerning the Four Truths and the Five Practices, one enters into a single thought-moment to constitute the perfect contemplation.

Third, relying on phenomena (*vastu*), as in the case of Rājagṛha and Gṛdhrakūṭa, which derive their names from actual entities; here, one borrows these phenomena as objects of contemplation to guide deluded attachments, as can be recognized in the examples of the Vaipulya scriptures and the Samantabhadra [chapter].
Question:
To which of the three meanings do the sixteen contemplations now belong?
Answer:
Since one does not grasp the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) to enter the mind and form a contemplation, it is clear that faith is not attached to phenomena.

Furthermore, since one does not rely on the meanings of those external events to establish the object (*ālambana*) or the contemplation, it is evident through verification that this is not based upon external events.
The Tathāgata directly expounds the gates of practice, realization, and cultivation for the sixteen contemplations; this is precisely the stage of "following the practice.
Question:

The three types [of contemplation] in the *Yili* (Exemplification of Meaning) are all contemplations of principle (*li*). Now, these sixteen [contemplations] sequentially rely upon the phenomena of the environment and its inhabitants (*yi-zheng shi*). How do they relate to those three types?
Answer:

Regarding the two types of threefold contemplation—those based on phenomena (*vastu*) and those attached to principles (*dharma*)—there are both phenomenal and noumenal aspects; let us set these aside for now. From the perspective of the threefold contemplation as practiced, for what reason can one not proceed through the phenomena sequentially?
Since it is stated that one proceeds from practice, there must necessarily be four types of practice.
Although the single method of constant sitting (*nitya-prahāṇa*) exclusively contemplates principle (*li*), how could the other three samādhis not also involve phenomena (*shi*)?

For instance, the three contemplations of the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi* involve the phenomenon of recollecting the Buddha; the three contemplations of the Vaipulya sūtras involve the phenomenon of upholding mantras; the three contemplations of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* involve the phenomenon of reciting the sūtra; the three contemplations of the *Avalokiteśvara-bodhisattva-pūrṇapraṇidhāna-sūtra* involve the phenomenon of counting the breath; and the three contemplations of the *Bodhyaṅga-samādhi* involve the phenomenon of the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*).
If these sequential practices do not arise from [the threefold] conduct, to what category do they belong?

In the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi*, one first contemplates the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel on the soles of the feet, proceeding in reverse order up to the mark of the *uṣṇīṣa* (cranial protuberance); when contemplating those marks, one employs the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).
Since that [previous case] was based on practice, why should this alone not be so?
Furthermore, the *Yili* states: "Contemplate the one mind within the myriad objects. How could the present [distinction between] the environment and its inhabitants (*yi-zheng*) not be the one mind?

While the sutra text lists the characteristics of the sixteen objects in full detail, the Great Master merely indicates the threefold perfect contemplation (*yuan san guan*) in the title, intending for one to use this contemplation to observe the sixteen objects; this is precisely what is meant by "although the myriad objects differ, the principle of the wondrous contemplation is equal."

Furthermore, if the three contemplations (*sanguan*) of the present [text] and the three contemplations of the various sequential practices were not "from-practice" (*cong xing*) and so forth, why would it be said that the meaning of the three contemplations consists of only these three types?
Question:

In this sutra, the passage regarding the contemplation of the image (*xiangguan*) alone states, "This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. Since none of the other passages contain words concerning the contemplation of principle (*liguan*), one knows that everything outside of the Buddha consists of the contemplation of phenomena (*shiguan*).
Even if one were to apply this principle to examine the fifteen [aspects], this would be the practitioner’s intent for employing contemplation based on principle (*li*).
According to the explicit text of the sutra, however, these are merely contemplations based on phenomena (*shi*).
Answer:

If one relies directly upon the sutras to cultivate contemplation and enter realization, why would it be necessary to explain the intent of the sutras and establish methods of contemplation based on the four reliances?

The Great Master deeply grasped the Buddha’s intent; therefore, in the opening title, he explained the contemplating subject through the wondrous three contemplations and the contemplated Buddha through the wondrous three bodies, stating: "Although the contemplations are sixteen, the term 'Buddha' already encompasses them all."
Now, relying on the Great Master’s use of the three sublime contemplations to observe the sixteen objects, how could this be merely the practitioner’s own subjective application of contemplation?

One should know that among the four kinds of samādhis, there is none that does not contemplate the principle of the Three Truths within phenomena; however, because the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi* and others rely on wholesome matters of both concentration and distraction, and the "Arousing of Mindfulness" (*bodhyanga*) freely engages with matters such as good and evil, they alone receive the designation of "traversing phenomena."

If one who practices constant sitting (*prahāṇa*) and so forth contemplates the three truths directly regarding the matters of the three paths, without concurrently cultivating wholesome deeds or indulging in unwholesome ones, they receive the name "receptive" (*anuloma*).
How could the method of contemplation in this sutra possibly differ from the four samādhis?
Thus, one should know that these sixteen [visualizations] are precisely the practice of conduct, the sequential engagement with objects, and the contemplation of principles.

It should be understood that all sixteen employ the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) as the method for their conceptual forms (*nimitta*). Because the three contemplations are subtle, one first contemplates the setting sun and clear water; as the three contemplations gradually become more manifest, one then contemplates the earth, trees, the seat-image, and the Buddha-body. All subsequent objects of focus must likewise be practiced through the three contemplations.
2. Below the heading "Regarding the Ten," the text provides a topical outline.
The sixteen contemplations are divided into three categories.
Those six belonging to the environment (*niśraya-vipāka*) consist of the sun, which indicates the direction for sending forth one's thoughts, and the ice, which represents the ground of lapis lazuli.

Although these objects belong to this land, they are intended to manifest the realm of that country; therefore, the first six contemplations are all its *parinirmita-āśraya* (environmental retribution).

As for the seventh being categorized as *samyag-vipāka* (proper retribution): the seat is the direct support for the three sages, and the images represent the true bodies of the three sages; therefore, the seventh contemplation is called proper retribution.

These three grades of people proceed from this world to that; because their cultivation of causes, their reliance on physical forms, and their phenomenal characteristics differ, these three constitute a single category. Second, from "The First" onwards, the text provides an explanation according to its topical divisions, which is threefold:

first, the six contemplations concerning the *pariṇāmanabhājanaloka* (the external environment), which are sixfold: 1. Contemplating the impurity of the body. 2. Contemplating the suffering of the world. 3. Contemplating the impermanence of conditioned things. 4. Contemplating the absence of self. 5. Contemplating the emptiness of phenomena. 6. Contemplating the signlessness of all dharmas. (To be continued...)
First, the Contemplation of the Sun, in two parts:
First, establishing the intent and dividing the sections.
One first performs the contemplation of the sun, intending to bind the mind [to it].
If the mind is generally dark and distracted, how can it clearly perceive the wondrous realm of the Pure Land?
Therefore, one is instructed to focus exclusively on the form of the setting sun.
By binding the mind to a single object and contemplating it without ceasing, the mind will then become concentrated.
If the mind is calm and subtle, all various methods of contemplation can be practiced.

Regarding the method of binding the mind that requires the visualization of the sun setting: this is intended to direct the concentrated thought toward the West, as that is the dwelling place of Amitābha.
II. Detailed Explanation, in two parts:
First, from "The Buddha said" onwards, there is the general exhortation to practice meditation.

Regarding the scriptural passage, "Vaidhī, you and all sentient beings," Vaidhī and others represent those currently capable of receiving the teaching (the present *adhikāra*), while "all sentient beings" refers to those who will be so in the future (the future *adhikāra*). Thus, we know that the practice of meditation is not restricted solely to the time of the Buddha's presence.

Moreover, since Vaidehī was the initiator who specifically requested the method for right reception on behalf of people of the present age, our Buddha therefore exhorted sentient beings to practice it.
How is this practice to be performed?
Focusing exclusively on a single location, namely the West.
Second, from "How... onwards, the main exposition of the visualization of the sun, in three parts:
first, presenting the object of observation.
The meaning of the scriptural passage is as follows: that which was previously seen, or the currently perceived appearance of the sun about to set, serves as the object of contemplation.

This visualization is universally applicable, with the sole exception of those born in the lower realms who are both blind; since they do not recognize the sun, they are unable to form a mental image of it.

If those who once possessed sight can still practice this even now as blind people, how much more so for those who currently possess sight and see the sun clearly; for them, it is even easier to practice.
One should take the setting sun that is actually seen as the object and contemplate it until the sun within the visualization arises.
Second, from "One should give rise to" (*dang qi*) onwards, the text correctly teaches contemplation.

The character "contemplation" (*guan*) in the title is explained as the three sublime contemplations (*san guan*). The title is the general [principle], while the sutra text is the specific; how could the general not permeate the specific?

Now, when one contemplates the setting sun, if one can contemplate it such that the contemplation proceeds in accordance with understanding, this is the concentration on phenomena (*vastu-samādhi*) of the Tripitaka Teaching;
herein, both the contemplating subject and the contemplated object are nothing other than arising and ceasing.
In the concentration on phenomena of the Shared Teaching, both the contemplating subject and the contemplated object are like illusions and transformations.
One discerns that the capacity for perception is fundamentally Buddha-nature.

Within the sequential contemplation of the perceiver and the perceived within perception, the person of perfect realization possesses a wondrous understanding that the mind capable of perception inherently contains all phenomena of both the environment and its inhabitants.

Now, by taking the sun of the fully realized mind as the object of the very mind that is the sun, one causes the sun of the original nature to manifest before oneself; this is precisely taking the realm of the dharma-realm as the object of the mind of the dharma-realm, thereby giving rise to the sun of the dharma-realm.
Since all things are the Dharma-realm, how could they not be identical to emptiness, the provisional, and the middle?

Even for a person of the Perfect Teaching who constantly encounters these through their six sense faculties, they must still realize them as identical to emptiness, the provisional, and the middle in every thought-moment; how then could one now abandon these three in the sudden practice of contemplation?
This is still a general indication.
If one were to discuss specifically the daily progress in accomplishing the three contemplations: because the faculties and their objects are empty and quiescent, the sun of the mind is unimpeded;
because they are provisionally established through dependent origination, the accumulation of thoughts arises daily.
Because their minds are daily the entire dharma-realm, they manifest within that very place.
These three contemplations are identical within a single mind; they are neither one nor three, yet they are both three and one—an inconceivable mystery.

Because all the practices and cultivations of a person of perfect penetration (yuanren) are entirely like this; if it were otherwise, it would not be the practice of the contemplation of phenomena (shiguan) by a person of perfect penetration.

A person of universal penetration (tongren) must cultivate various samādhis of phenomena with a mind that is like an illusion, thereby verifying that the person of perfect penetration employs the very center of the mind to accomplish the contemplation of phenomena.

Having used the wondrous mind to contemplate the setting sun, this mind becomes firmly established and is able to manifest the appearance of the sun within its own nature; it is not only visible when the eyes are closed, but is also clearly perceived when the eyes are open.
If it is thus, then the daily contemplation is accomplished.
The Commentary sets forth two meanings;
first, from "The Teaching and Command" onwards, it removes doubts.
The lower scroll of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "If there are sentient beings who, with a mind of doubt, cultivate various meritorious virtues and vow to be born in that land;
or those who, failing to understand the Buddha’s wisdom, cultivate the roots of goodness and vow to be born in that land."
These sentient beings are born in those palaces with a lifespan of five hundred years; they constantly do not see the Buddha, do not hear the Dharma, and do not see the Sangha.
In that land, they undergo birth from a womb.

"This person lacked wisdom in past lives, which resulted from their state of doubt; even though they were born in that celestial palace, they did not harbor a single thought of evil, yet for five hundred years they did not see the Triple Gem."

Regarding the phrase "one intentionally forms this contemplation to eliminate doubt and confusion," the Sūtra states: "If one does not understand the Buddha’s wisdom, then doubt and confusion arise. The Commentary states: "One intentionally forms this contemplation to eliminate doubt and confusion. This clearly demonstrates that this contemplation is capable of understanding the Buddha’s wisdom.

If one does not employ the threefold contemplation within a single mind to contemplate the setting sun, then one is deluded regarding the Buddha’s wisdom; how, then, could this contemplation be said to eliminate doubt and confusion?

Since this is the case for the contemplation of the sun, it follows by analogy for all other contemplations; thus we know that the Great Master established these present methods of contemplation based upon the Buddha’s wisdom.
However, because the sixteen contemplations belong to the Sudden Teaching (dun-jiao), they employ Buddha-wisdom from beginning to end.

If ordinary or Hinayana practitioners possess wholesome roots, they should dedicate them toward Buddha-wisdom at the time of death; those who have committed various evils must rely on Buddha-wisdom to seek the eradication of their karmic obstacles. These individuals are also said to have "comprehended Buddha-wisdom" and are free from doubt and confusion.

Since there are those who possess the seed of the vehicle and are born there, they will swiftly behold the Buddha, hear the Dharma, and join the assembly of the ocean-like multitude; they shall not be born in borderlands or from a womb.
Second, from the words "The Obstacles," below, follows the elimination of obstacles.
This refers precisely to the grave offenses of the five *ānantarya* sins.
Because the power of the "scattered" virtues in that sutra is weak, such perverse slanders do not arise there.

Therefore, that sutra states: "If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing its name, give rise to faith and joy, and even for a single thought-moment direct their minds with sincerity toward rebirth in that land, they shall immediately attain rebirth and abide in the stage of non-retrogression."
"Except for those who have committed the five heinous crimes or slandered the true Dharma.
If one relies on this sutra to cultivate correct contemplation, even down to the visualization of the sun, one will be able to extinguish the grave sins of the five heinous crimes.
Thus we know that the attainment of birth [in the Pure Land] despite having committed grave offenses must necessarily depend on the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

Regarding the "Discourse on the Lower Grade" itself, the contemplation for the lower grade of the lower birth states that one "eliminates the sins of birth and death for eighty billion kalpas"; the present mention of "sixty" is likely a scribal error for the character "six."
Question:

Since one uses the dharma-realm as the object of the mind to manifest the sun of the dharma-realm, such that one constantly sees the sun whether with eyes closed or open, this is the practice of contemplation (vipaśyanā) seeing the principle of the dharma-realm; it corresponds to the middle three grades.
Question: Why is it now determined that its position is at the beginning of the "names" stage, belonging to the lowest-of-the-low grade?
Answer:

Regarding the characteristics of the contemplation of principle and the stabilization of phenomena, although the practitioner’s mind is non-dual, because phenomena are still intermingled with ordinary delusions, the afflictions have not yet been subdued; thus, the stabilization of phenomena can only be achieved [at this level].

When the contemplation of principle causes the forgetting of emotions, the subduing of delusions then begins to manifest; thus, the initial subduing of distinct delusions is called the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-bhūmi*), wherein one perceives the principle of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). When these are deeply subdued, it is called the stage of semblance (*pratirūpa-bhūmi*), wherein one perceives [the realm]. Only upon their partial severance does one attain true vision of the Dharma-realm.

Those who practice today observe the sun, ice, and lapis lazuli; although they employ the mind and objects of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) in their contemplation, their delusions remain entirely unsubdued and mundane sentiments are still thick. They have merely attained the "name-and-word" stage of seeing the sun of the Dharma-realm, which does not yet constitute the stage of contemplative practice (vipaśyanā-bhūmi).

This judgment was made primarily for those of dull faculties; it is because they obtain the benefit of a concentrated mind through provisional mental imagery during the contemplation of the sun and so forth that this stage is placed within the "name-and-word" (nāmamātra) phase.

If one possesses sharp faculties, the Dharma-realm is revealed as the sun, whereby they are able to completely subdue and spontaneously eliminate the two kinds of coarse afflictions—how could this not be the sun-contemplation passing through the nine grades?
Question:

Now, although one may understand through reasoning that the visualization of the Buddha appears before one's eyes and that, even if afflictions have not yet been severed, the practice is already established, this cannot be equated with the concentrated mind that perceives the sun.

This is based on the explanation in the sutra below: "Those of the lowest-of-the-low capacity, being oppressed by suffering, have no leisure to recollect the Buddha; they merely utter the name of that Buddha for the duration of ten recitations. Although their minds are continuous, it ultimately cannot be categorized as the concentrated mind that sees the sun.
Why are they all together in the ninth grade?
Answer:

Because they committed the heinous offenses and performed various evil deeds, they were oppressed by suffering at the moment of death; yet they encountered virtuous friends who expounded the sublime Dharma for them.
Although one cannot contemplate the three bodies of that Buddha, because of fear of the hells, one fervently calls his name with ten complete recitations.
Having severed subsequent evil, one immediately relies on this mindfulness to take rebirth within that lotus; this is termed the lowest of the lower grades.

Now, as this treatise begins, one who delights in practicing samādhi and associating with virtuous friends hears that the mind inherently possesses the various phenomena of the Pure Land, both the environment and its inhabitants; thus, they set their intention upon fully cultivating the sixteen contemplative methods, and therefore first contemplate the sun to cause the mind to dwell firmly.
Looking back at the various grades of contemplation, this belongs to the final category.

Although such a person may not yet achieve meditative concentration (samādhi) through the practice of the matter, they are able to recite the Buddha's name ten times without distraction; thus, they are also encompassed by concentration. Furthermore, because they possess the power of courageous resolve at the moment of death, they are able to be included in the ninth grade.
Therefore, although the modes of practice differ slightly, there is no distinction in their levels.
Third, from "This is called" onwards is the conclusion.
Second, the contemplation of water, in two parts:
First, the division into sections (two).
Second, the detailed explanation (three):
first, presenting the object of observation.
One takes as the object of focus the waters of a large pond previously seen.
Second, from the phrase "seeing the water" onwards, the text correctly explains the actual cultivation of contemplation.

Having received the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong), one knows that the mind capable of conceptualization is endowed with the nature of the seven great elements; therefore, by means of the mind that possesses water, one entrusts itself to the water that is identical to the mind, contemplating its original nature so that the water manifests before one, and further causing all its various characteristics to manifest within the contemplation of the mind-nature.
The text consists of four parts:
first, the visualization of water.
Once the wondrous mind is set in motion, the water of its nature arises; by focusing the visualization on its clarity, one prevents the mind from scattering.
2. From "Having already seen" onwards, water is transformed into ice.
Since the dharmas inherent in the nature (xingju) transform with absolute freedom, one can cause water to become solid water.
3. Below "Seeing Ice," the ice is transformed into lapis lazuli.
If the perception of ice is perfected, the lapis lazuli can be recognized.
4. Below "This Perception," one contemplates the lapis lazuli as becoming the ground.
The mind-treasury is endowed with all dharmas; how could it have any limits?
Yet, lacking the conditions for sublime contemplation, they remain hidden and do not manifest.

Now, by relying on the Buddha’s words and contemplating them in accordance with their true nature, various wondrous signs, such as the radiance of the jewel-ground, appear in accordance with the mind.
This consists of six sections:
first, the ground becomes transparently clear;
second, from "Below" onwards, the radiance of the jeweled banners.
3. From "Lapis lazuli" downward: the adornment of the ground. 4.
From "Each and every" downward: the jeweled light pavilions. 5.
From "Upon the platform" downward: flower banners and musical instruments.
Sixth: Below the section on the "Eight Kinds," the wind-instruments perform the Dharma.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase "In reality, there are no seasons" and so forth, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "There are no four seasons there; it is neither cold nor hot."
Furthermore, where there are neither sun nor moon, there is constant radiance.
Because this land relies upon the eight kinds of winds from the four cardinal and four intermediate directions, it likewise possesses eight winds in correspondence with these.
However, those eight winds do not cause things to grow or decay as they do in this land; rather, they merely play the music of spontaneity and manifest the sounds of the wondrous Dharma.
3. "This is" and below is the conclusion.
Third, the contemplation of the stages (bhūmi), in two parts:
first, the division of sections.
Second, the detailed explanation has four parts.

First, regarding "gradual visualization": one transforms the perception of ice to manifest lapis lazuli; yet, although one contemplates the various adornments of the ground, it still does not accord with the supreme abode of that Buddha’s transformation body.
This is because the three contemplations are still subtle and still involve provisional mental imagery; therefore, at that stage, it is termed "coarse vision.
Second, from "If one attains" onwards, is the contemplation of reality.
Through the manifest power of wondrous contemplation, one achieves success in samādhi and beholds the land upon which that supreme body relies; how could its adorned features be fully described?
One should understand that the Land of Common Residence inherently possesses the three lands in a horizontal manner, and its characteristics are by no means few.

As stated in various sutras, when ordinary or Hinayana practitioners dedicate their virtuous deeds toward seeking rebirth, even if they rely upon the Mahayana, these remain merely scattered virtues; consequently, the resulting environment of the Pure Land remains comparatively inferior.
If the subtle essence of mental contemplation in the Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao) is now considered, the pure marks perceived therein are forever distinct from those of other schools.

For instance, when practicing the sublime contemplation within this defiled Land of Common Dwelling, one may still perceive the Exalted Special Body and the Land of True Reward; how then could the bodies and lands of the Pure Land of Common Dwelling be regarded as uniform?
Therefore, now that the Samādhi of the Sublime Perception of the Earth has been accomplished, the manifestations of its adornments are such that they cannot be fully described.
Third, from "The Buddha said" onwards, the benefits are clarified.

The Commentary states: "The preceding water is perception" means that this refers to the phenomenon of water turning to ice in this world to represent that jewel-ground; because it is merely a conceptual construction, it is called a "coarse vision."
Now, when one achieves samādhi and truly perceives that ground, it is called "actual contemplation" (*bhūtamanasikāra*).

To say that "conceptual visualization cannot extinguish transgressions" is the Great Master’s method of exhorting practitioners in accordance with the sūtras, intended to cause them to quickly achieve samādhi;
it does not mean that conceptual visualization is entirely incapable of extinguishing transgressions.
How is this known to be so?

Even the daily contemplation—which is comparable to the lower grade of the lowest birth—eliminates a certain number of offenses; how much more so for one who has a coarse perception of the ground, which would not eliminate transgressions at all?
Fourth, from "performing this" onwards, the text clarifies the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox.
If one’s contemplation accords with the sutras, it is called "seeing in accordance with nature" (*dharmatā-darśana*) and is termed "right contemplation.
If one’s perception of signs contradicts the sutras, it gives rise to demonic activity and is thus termed "erroneous contemplation.
This shall apply to all subsequent sections as well.
IV. Contemplation of the Tree, in two parts:
First, the division of sections;
Second, the detailed explanation, in three parts:
First, connecting the preceding with the subsequent.
Second, the actual elucidation of the contemplative practice.
Question:
Question: The contemplations on the sun and water both first establish an objective referent (*ālambana*); why then is this not said for the contemplations on the earth, trees, and so forth?
Answer:
To speak specifically, the sun and water possess previously perceived characteristics (*nimitta*) that can be pointed out as objective referents.
Since the trees on the ground have already ceased to exist and are no longer perceived, what can serve as their object?
If one discusses this in general terms, all things may be considered objects. Why is this so?

All contemplations take the characteristics shown by the teachings as their basis; they are held in mind as the objects of focus. Furthermore, one realizes that the contemplating subject itself inherently possesses these dharmas. By relying on the object, the visualization is perfected, causing the dharmas inherent in one's nature to manifest within the mind and eyes. Therefore, the mental contemplation and the characteristics it produces each possess the threefold nature.
Thus, it is known that, according to the general discussion, all possess an objective domain (*ālambana*).
This text consists of five parts;
first, from "Contemplating the Jewels" onwards, the physical structures below the tree, as well as their adornments and the phenomena of their arising, are all the supported (*āśrita*).
Now, each individual tree is eight thousand *yojanas* in height; this constitutes its essential substance (*āśraya*).
Second, from "each one" onwards, follows the description of its adornments.

Regarding *vaiḍūrya*—its full form is *vaiḍūryaja*, which translates as "not far away"—this refers to a mountain in the Western Regions located not far from the city of Vārāṇasī; since this gem originates there, it is named after that place.
"Glass" (bōlí) is correctly transliterated as *sphāṭika*; its appearance somewhat resembles that of crystal (*śilājatu*) in this region, though there are also red and white varieties.
Third, from "the various devas" onwards, it clarifies the arising of phenomena.
"Born" refers to sentient beings, specifically the youths of the various devas.
When "birth" is contrasted with all matters of adornment, they are all termed "dharmas.

*Śakrābhilagna* is translated here as "the victorious maṇi"; its correct form is *maṇi*, which is translated as "free from defilement," meaning that the light of this jewel is pure and not stained by impurities.
Furthermore, it is translated as "increasing," meaning that wherever this jewel exists, its virtuous accomplishments will necessarily increase.
The older translations, such as "transforming into what is wished for" (*yìruì suīyì*), are all semantic translations.
Regarding "the most excellent among colors," this refers to the light of mani-jewels interspersed with various gems; its color and form are so exquisite that nothing surpasses it.

As for "Jambūnada gold": *jambū* is fully transliterated as *rǎnbù nàtó*; this is the name of a river in the Western Regions, located near the Jambūnada tree, and the gold originates from within that river.
Thus, the river derives its name from the tree, and the gold is named after the river.
It is like the "Vessel of Śakra" (Śakraka-ghaṭa): "Śakra" is fully called Śakra-indra, which means "Capable Lord," signifying that he is able to act as the Lord of Devas.
Regarding the term "jar," the *Śāstra* (Treatise), chapter fifteen, states: "There was a man who constantly made offerings to a deity.
This man was poor, yet for twelve full years he made offerings with single-minded devotion, seeking wealth and nobility."
The deva took pity on this person, manifested his own form, and asked him:
"What do you seek?
He replied:
"I seek wealth and honor, desiring that all my wishes be fulfilled.
The deity gave him a vessel called the "Vase of Virtue" (Guṇakumbha) and said to him:
"Whatever things you require shall emerge from this vase."
"Once that person has done so, they shall obtain whatever their heart desires, with nothing remaining unattained.
Now, these wonderful flowers emerge bearing various fruits, just as that celestial vase produces all manner of objects; therefore, it is used as a metaphor for this.
4. From "There is greatness" (*mahat*) onwards, the Buddha-land is manifested.
It is not only a single great trichiliocosm that is manifested; the Buddha-fields of the ten directions are also manifested therein.
If the contemplation of the trees is successfully developed, then contemplating the Buddha-lands should likewise not be difficult.
5. "Contemplating and Seeing" below concludes the visualization.
Although one sees the lands of the ten directions by means of the light-canopy, since [the vision] arose from the tree, it is necessary to conclude the visualization by returning to its source.
3. "This is" and below concludes [the section].
This concludes the fourth visualization regarding the tree.
5. Visualization of the Ponds, in two parts:
First, the outline of the commentary.
Second, the exegesis of the sutra, in five parts:
first, clarifying the substance of the ponds; the meaning of "substance" is the same as that of the trees.
2. From "Each one" onwards, the characteristics of the ponds are clarified.
The branching golden channels, the sandy bottoms, and the lotus flowers are all marvelous features of the eight ponds.
Third, the section beginning with "Its water" (*qi mo*) clarifies that [the tree] accords with the mind.
Regarding this precious water, it is said to be suited to human sentiment; it naturally rises into the tree and subsequently flows downward.
Therefore, the *Sūtra on the Ascent to Tuṣita* clarifies that there are waters flowing among the beams and rafters of the Tuṣita palace;
this is the same as here. Fourth, from "Its sound" onwards, it clarifies the benefits.
Thus, the sound of water preaches the Dharma, increasing the contemplative wisdom of people.
